lessons.title: Choose one number for position
lessons.idea: A coordinate is a number that tells us where something is.
body: A bead on a straight wire needs one position number. Choose a zero and call the position q. Positive q means right of zero; negative q means left. This describes where the bead is. It does not yet tell us how the bead moves.
lessons.equation: q = signed position along the wire

equationGuide.meaning: A bead on a straight wire needs one position number. Choose a zero and call the position q. Positive q means right of zero; negative q means left. This describes where the bead is. It does not yet tell us how the bead moves.

example.title: A bead on a wire
steps: Mark zero at the left end of a straight wire.
The bead is 2 metres to the right of zero, so q = 2 m.

lessons.title: Use a rule that limits the motion
lessons.idea: A constraint is a rule that limits where an object can go.
body: A bead on a rigid circular wire must stay on that circle. Its two position numbers, x and y, cannot change freely. The circle rule links them. R is the circle’s radius, measured from its centre.

equationGuide.meaning: A bead on a rigid circular wire must stay on that circle. Its two position numbers, x and y, cannot change freely. The circle rule links them. R is the circle’s radius, measured from its centre.

example.title: A bead on the upper half of a circle
steps: Use a circle with radius R = 5 m. The bead has x = 3 m.
Then y² = 25 − 9 = 16 m². On the upper half, y = 4 m.

lessons.title: Subtract stored energy from motion energy
lessons.idea: The Lagrangian combines two energies by subtracting them.
body: Call motion energy T and potential energy V. Potential energy is stored because of position or shape. For the simple systems here, the Lagrangian L is T minus V. It helps us find motion in later steps. It is different from total energy, which adds them.

equationGuide.meaning: Call motion energy T and potential energy V. Potential energy is stored because of position or shape. For the simple systems here, the Lagrangian L is T minus V. It helps us find motion in later steps. It is different from total energy, which adds them.

example.title: One instant of a moving cart
steps: The cart has T = 9 joules and V = 4 joules.
Its Lagrangian is L = 9 − 4 = 5 joules.

lessons.title: Add the Lagrangian over time
lessons.idea: Action adds the Lagrangian along a whole motion.
body: Call action S. If L stays constant, multiply it by the time taken. If L changes, split the time into tiny pieces and add their contributions. That continuous adding is an integral. Action belongs to a whole path over time, not just one instant.
lessons.equation: For constant L: S = L × elapsed time

equationGuide.meaning: Call action S. If L stays constant, multiply it by the time taken. If L changes, split the time into tiny pieces and add their contributions. That continuous adding is an integral. Action belongs to a whole path over time, not just one instant.

example.title: A constant contribution
steps: A path has L = 3 J throughout 2 seconds.
Its action is S = 3 × 2 = 6 J·s.

lessons.terms: Action (S): The Lagrangian added over a time interval. J·s: Joule-second: the unit of action. Integral: A way to add contributions that may change continuously.

glossary.definition: The Lagrangian added over a time interval.

lessons.limits: The multiplication shown is exact only when L is constant over the interval. In general, S = ∫ L dt.

lessons.title: Look for no first-order change
lessons.idea: The physical path makes action stationary under small allowed changes.
body: Keep the start and finish positions and times fixed. Slightly bend the path in between. Stationary means the action has no change proportional to that tiny bend. Smaller, squared changes may remain. This rule does not always mean the action is the smallest possible value.
lessons.equation: stationary action: first-order change in S = 0

example.title: A toy action near a path
steps: Let ε measure a small path change, with S = (5 + ε²) J·s.
At ε = 0, there is no term proportional to ε. The first-order change is zero.

lessons.terms: Stationary: Having zero first-order change; not necessarily being a minimum. First-order change: The part proportional to a small change, rather than its square. ε (epsilon): Here, a unit-free number measuring a small change of path.

glossary.definition: Having zero first-order change; not necessarily being a minimum.

lessons.title: Turn the action rule into motion
lessons.idea: The Euler–Lagrange rule turns a Lagrangian into an equation of motion.
body: For a cart on an ideal spring, the rule gives m × a = −k × q. Here q is distance from rest, a is acceleration, m is mass and k is spring stiffness. The minus sign points the acceleration back toward rest. The calculus steps are in the optional detail.

Write the position as q and its rate as q̇. In the equation below, ∂ means a derivative while holding the other input fixed. First differentiate with respect to the velocity, then take its time derivative. Subtract the derivative with respect to position. Setting this to zero gives the spring’s motion rule.
lessons.equation:
L = ½m q̇² − ½k q²
d/dt(∂L/∂q̇) − ∂L/∂q = 0
m a − (−kq) = 0
m a = −kq

equationGuide.meaning: For a cart on an ideal spring, the rule gives m × a = −k × q. Here q is distance from rest, a is acceleration, m is mass and k is spring stiffness. The minus sign points the acceleration back toward rest. The calculus steps are in the optional detail.

example.title: A cart pulled back by its spring
steps: Let m = 2 kg, k = 8 N/m and q = 0.5 m.
Then a = −8 × 0.5 ÷ 2 = −2 m/s², back toward q = 0.

lessons.limits: This uses one dimension, constant mass and an ideal linear spring, with no friction or driving force.

lessons.title: Turn an angular rate into a speed
lessons.idea: A longer pendulum moves farther for the same change of angle.
body: An ideal pendulum is a small mass on a light, rigid rod. Use its angle θ from straight down as the position number. A dot over θ means its rate of change. Multiply the size of that angular rate by the rod length ℓ to find the speed.

equationGuide.meaning: An ideal pendulum is a small mass on a light, rigid rod. Use its angle θ from straight down as the position number. A dot over θ means its rate of change. Multiply the size of that angular rate by the rod length ℓ to find the speed.

example.title: One turning pendulum
steps: The rod is ℓ = 2 m long. The angular rate is θ̇ = −1.5 rad/s.
Speed is 2 × 1.5 = 3 m/s. The minus sign gives the turning direction, not a negative speed.

lessons.title: Write motion energy using the angle rate
lessons.idea: The pendulum’s motion energy can be written using its angle rate.
body: Motion energy is half the mass times speed squared. Replace speed by rod length times angular rate. This gives a formula using the position choice we want: the angle. Squaring the angular rate makes the energy nonnegative in either turning direction.

lessons.title: Measure stored energy from the lowest point
lessons.idea: Raising a pendulum above its lowest point adds gravitational potential energy.
body: Choose zero stored energy at the bottom of the swing. At angle θ, the mass has risen by ℓ times one minus cos θ. Multiply that height by mass m and gravitational acceleration g. This gives the potential energy V relative to the bottom.
lessons.equation: V = m × g × ℓ × (1 − cos θ)

lessons.title: Hold the other input fixed
lessons.idea: A partial derivative changes one input while holding the others fixed.
body: A Lagrangian can depend on position q and velocity q̇. When finding its change with position, hold velocity fixed. The motion-energy term then stays unchanged. For an ideal spring, only the position-energy term contributes to this derivative.
lessons.equation:
L = ½m q̇² − ½k q²
At fixed q̇: ∂L/∂q = −kq

steps: For a spring, take k = 6 N/m and q = 0.5 m. Hold q̇ fixed.

lessons.title: Find the pendulum’s angular acceleration
lessons.idea: The pendulum’s angular acceleration points back toward the bottom.
body: For this Lagrangian, differentiating with respect to θ̇ gives mℓ²θ̇. Taking its time derivative gives mℓ²θ̈. The partial derivative with respect to θ is −mgℓ sin θ. Subtract the latter in the Euler–Lagrange rule, then divide by mℓ². The steps below all belong to the same pendulum model.
lessons.equation:
L = ½mℓ²θ̇² − mgℓ(1 − cos θ)
d/dt(∂L/∂θ̇) − ∂L/∂θ = 0
mℓ²θ̈ + mgℓ sin θ = 0
θ̈ = −(g/ℓ) sin θ

equationGuide.meaning: Put the pendulum’s motion energy and stored energy into L = T − V. The Euler–Lagrange rule then gives θ̈ = −(g/ℓ) sin θ. Two dots mean angular acceleration. For a small positive angle, the negative result turns the motion back toward zero. The mass cancels out.

example.title: Acceleration at one angle
steps: Use g = 10 m/s², ℓ = 2 m and θ = π/6 rad, where sin θ = 0.5.

lessons.terms: θ̈ (theta double dot): Angular acceleration: how quickly the angular rate changes. sin θ: Sine of the angle from straight down. Euler–Lagrange rule: The rule that finds motion from the Lagrangian.

glossary.definition: Angular acceleration: how quickly the angular rate changes.

lessons.title: Combine two quantities with a Poisson bracket
lessons.idea: A Poisson bracket combines the position and momentum slopes of two quantities.
body: If f has no explicit time input, its rate along a Hamiltonian trajectory is its Poisson bracket with H. The first two relations below recover the two Hamilton equations. The final relation is the bracket calculated in this lesson’s single example.

equationGuide.meaning: Take two quantities f and g that depend on q and p. Multiply the position slope of f by the momentum slope of g. Subtract the reverse pairing. This calculation is called their Poisson bracket. Using H as the second quantity gives a motion rule for the first.

example.title: Bracket of position squared and momentum
steps: Choose f = q² and g = p. The four slopes are 2q, 1, 0 and 0 in the order used above.
Their bracket is 2q × 1 − 0 × 0 = 2q.
At q = 3 m, the bracket is 6 m.

lessons.terms: Poisson bracket ({f, g}): The two-product difference of slopes shown in the equation. f and g: Two quantities expressed as functions of position and paired momentum. Partial derivative: A slope with one input while the other input is held fixed.

glossary.definition: The two-product difference of slopes shown in the equation.

lessons.title: Account for an accelerating origin
lessons.idea: A free cart appears to accelerate opposite to an accelerating origin.
body: The cart has L = ½m(q̇ + ȧ)² in the moving coordinate. Its momentum derivative is d[m(q̇ + ȧ)]/dt = m(q̈ + ä). There is no q term, so the Euler–Lagrange equation sets this to zero. This reproduces the relative-acceleration rule.

lessons.title: Let a moving support transfer energy
lessons.idea: A moving constraint can do work on the object it supports.
body: Power is force times velocity in the force’s direction. A support pushing upward on a bead that moves upward gives it energy. If the bead moves downward while the force is upward, that force takes energy away. A frictionless support is not necessarily a support that does no work.

lessons.title: Find the speed toward or away from the centre
lessons.idea: Energy left after the effective potential sets the radial speed.
body: Radial motion changes the distance r from the centre. At fixed angular momentum, subtract the effective potential from total energy E. The remainder is radial kinetic energy. It must be nonnegative. The square root gives the speed; inward or outward motion supplies its sign.

lessons.title: Find the radius of a circular orbit
lessons.idea: A circular orbit sits at a stationary point of the effective potential.
body: At fixed angular momentum p_φ, V_eff = −α/r + p_φ²/(2mr²). Its derivative is α/r² − p_φ²/(mr³). Setting this to zero and multiplying by r³ gives αr = p_φ²/m. The positive solution is the circular radius.

equationGuide.meaning: A circle keeps r fixed, so the radial force must balance the turning term. For attraction with V = −α/r, setting the effective-potential slope to zero gives the radius below. Here α sets the attraction strength and p_φ is the fixed angular momentum.

example.title: One circular orbit
steps: Use p_φ = 4 kg·m²/s, m = 2 kg and α = 4 J·m.
The circular radius is r₀ = 4² ÷ (2 × 4) = 2 m.

lessons.terms: α (alpha): The positive constant in V = −α/r, measured in joule metres. J: Angular momentum about the force centre, in kilograms times metres squared per second. r₀: The circular-orbit radius.

glossary.definition: The positive constant in V = −α/r, measured in joule metres.

The circular-orbit radius.

lessons.title: Check whether a circular orbit resists a small radial nudge
lessons.idea: A minimum of the effective potential gives radial stability.
body: Look at the second derivative of V_eff at the circular radius. Call this curvature K_r. A positive value produces a restoring radial force after a small displacement. A negative value pushes the orbit farther away. If it is zero, this test alone cannot decide.

lessons.title: Use a matrix for three-dimensional rotation
lessons.idea: The inertia tensor turns angular velocity into angular momentum.
body: For point masses measured from the reference point, I_xx = Σm(y² + z²), while I_xy = −Σmxy. The other entries follow by exchanging x, y and z. This explains why off-diagonal terms can appear even though every mass is positive.

equationGuide.meaning: A tensor here is a three-by-three matrix. It records how the mass distribution responds to turning in different directions. Multiply it by the angular-velocity vector to get angular momentum L_rot. The two vectors need not point in the same direction.

example.title: One matrix multiplication
steps: Then L_rot = (6, −2, 0) kg·m²/s. It does not point along ω.

lessons.idea: In principal axes, rotational energy is a sum of three squared-rate terms.
body: Each principal direction contributes half its moment of inertia times its angular-velocity component squared. Add the three contributions. Reversing one component’s sign does not change its energy contribution. This is rotational energy; motion of the centre of mass may add more.

lessons.title: Follow the turning rates in body-fixed axes
lessons.idea: Euler’s equations include the effect of the axes rotating with the body.
body: The three equations are I₁ω̇₁ = τ₁ + (I₂ − I₃)ω₂ω₃, I₂ω̇₂ = τ₂ + (I₃ − I₁)ω₃ω₁, and I₃ω̇₃ = τ₃ + (I₁ − I₂)ω₁ω₂. Together they give the body-frame rates. They come from the inertial torque rule after accounting for the turning basis.

equationGuide.meaning: Axes painted on the body turn with it. In those axes, angular-velocity components can change even when external torque is zero. Euler’s equation for the first component includes the product of the other two components. Similar equations hold after cycling the labels 1, 2 and 3.

lessons.title: Identify the unstable spin axis
lessons.idea: Torque-free spin about the intermediate principal axis is unstable.
body: Order three distinct positive principal moments from smallest to largest. A small wobble around spin about the smallest or largest axis stays small. Around the middle axis it can grow. An exactly steady middle-axis spin is possible, but it does not resist small disturbances.

Intermediate-axis spin (I₂): unstable

lessons.title: See why doubling a displacement may not double a force
lessons.idea: A nonlinear force does not have to grow in direct proportion to displacement.
body: An ideal spring has force −kq. Add a cubic term −βq³ and the rule becomes nonlinear. Doubling q doubles the first term but multiplies the cubic term by eight. Adding two solutions is no longer a reliable way to get another solution.

lessons.title: Read an arrow in phase space
lessons.idea: The motion equations give an arrow at each position–momentum pair.
body: A phase portrait shows how a state moves through position q and momentum p. The arrow has components q̇ and ṗ. At positive q with p = 0 in an ideal spring, position is momentarily still but momentum starts decreasing. This tells us the direction of the nearby path.
lessons.equation:
For an ideal spring:
q̇ = p/m, ṗ = −kq

lessons.title: Trace a pendulum’s constant-energy path
lessons.idea: An undriven, frictionless pendulum follows a constant-energy curve in phase space.
body: Use angle θ and its paired angular momentum p_θ. The first energy term comes from motion; the second comes from height above the bottom. During ideal motion their sum stays fixed. Different energy values make different curves on the phase portrait.
lessons.equation: H(θ, p_θ) = p_θ²/(2mℓ²) + mgℓ(1 − cos θ)

lessons.title: Compare swing energy with the top of the pendulum
lessons.idea: The energy needed to reach the upright position separates swinging from full rotation.
body: The upright mass is 2ℓ above the bottom. Its potential energy is therefore 2mgℓ. Below this energy, a moving pendulum swings back and forth. Above it, the ideal rigid-rod pendulum can keep turning around. The boundary case needs its own careful look.

lessons.idea: The separatrix is the phase-space boundary between swings and rotations.

lessons.title: Add a repeating drive to the pendulum

body: A motor can repeatedly push the pendulum. In this model A sets the drive’s angular-acceleration size and Ω sets its timing. The term −γθ̇ represents damping. The drive can add or remove energy depending on the motion and its timing.

lessons.title: Look once per drive cycle
lessons.idea: Sampling at the same drive phase makes repeated patterns easier to see.
body: For a driven pendulum, record its angle and angular rate after each full drive period T_d. These points form a Poincaré section. A settled response that repeats every drive cycle gives one point; a response repeating every two cycles gives two points.

equationGuide.meaning: For a driven pendulum, record its angle and angular rate after each full drive period T_d. These points form a Poincaré section. A settled response that repeats every drive cycle gives one point; a response repeating every two cycles gives two points.

steps: The drive period is T_d = 2 s and the first recorded phase is at t = 0.
The next samples are at 2 s, 4 s and 6 s.

lessons.title: Measure how nearby motions separate
lessons.idea: Chaotic motion can make a tiny starting difference grow rapidly.
body: Compare two nearby states using the same fixed scales for angle and angular rate. Their separation δ can initially grow roughly as an exponential. The growth rate λ is called a Lyapunov exponent when defined over long motion with the proper limiting procedure. Brief growth alone is not proof of chaos.
lessons.equation:
For a local growth estimate:
δ(t) ≈ δ₀ exp(λt)

equationGuide.meaning: Compare two nearby states using the same fixed scales for angle and angular rate. Their separation δ can initially grow roughly as an exponential. The growth rate λ is called a Lyapunov exponent when defined over long motion with the proper limiting procedure. Brief growth alone is not proof of chaos.

example.title: Estimate a growing difference
steps: Let δ₀ = 0.001 and suppose separation doubles each second over this short interval.
After 2 s, the estimate is δ = 0.001 × 2² = 0.004.

lessons.title: Change position and momentum as a matched pair
lessons.idea: A canonical change of variables keeps Hamilton’s equations in their usual form.
body: For one pair, a smooth change is canonical when the new variables have Poisson bracket {Q, P} = 1. If position is scaled by a nonzero constant a, scale momentum by its reciprocal. Scaling both by the same factor usually fails this test.
lessons.equation:
Q = aq, P = p/a
{Q, P} = a × (1/a) = 1

equationGuide.meaning: For one pair, a smooth change is canonical when the new variables have Poisson bracket {Q, P} = 1. If position is scaled by a nonzero constant a, scale momentum by its reciprocal. Scaling both by the same factor usually fails this test.

example.title: Scale a pair together
steps: Use a = 2, q = 3 m and p = 8 kg·m/s.
The new pair is Q = 6 m and P = 4 kg·m/s. Their bracket is still 1.

lessons.title: Rewrite H using the new variables
lessons.idea: A time-independent canonical change rewrites the same Hamiltonian in new variables.
body: For Q = aq and P = p/a, solve backward: q = Q/a and p = aP. Substitute those expressions into H. For a free cart, the new function K is a²P²/(2m). It describes the same motion using the new pair.
lessons.equation:
K(Q, P) = H(Q/a, aP)
For a free cart: K = a²P²/(2m)

steps: Use a = 2, P = 3 kg·m/s and m = 2 kg.
K = 2² × 3² ÷ (2 × 2) = 9 J. The old momentum is p = 6 kg·m/s, giving the same energy.

lessons.title: Generate both variable rules from one function
lessons.idea: A generating function can give both parts of a canonical transformation.
body: A type-2 generating function F₂ uses the old position q and new momentum P. Differentiate it with respect to q to get old momentum p. Differentiate it with respect to P to get new position Q. These two derivatives make a matched transformation.

example.title: Generate the scaling transformation
steps: Choose F₂ = 2qP. Its derivatives give p = 2P and Q = 2q.
At q = 3 m and P = 2 kg·m/s, the pair is Q = 6 m and p = 4 kg·m/s.

lessons.terms: Generating function F₂: An action-valued function whose derivatives define a canonical change. Type 2: The convention using old position and new momentum as inputs. Action units: Energy multiplied by time, or momentum multiplied by position.

lessons.title: Include the extra term when the transformation changes with time
lessons.idea: A time-dependent canonical transformation changes the Hamiltonian by a time-derivative term.
body: Use the translating coordinate Q = q − ut, where u is constant. The generator F₂ = (q − ut)P gives p = P. Its time derivative is −uP. Add that term to the old free-cart Hamiltonian. The result produces the velocity measured from the moving origin.
lessons.equation:
K = H + ∂F₂/∂t
For F₂ = (q − ut)P: K = P²/(2m) − uP

equationGuide.meaning: Use the translating coordinate Q = q − ut, where u is constant. The generator F₂ = (q − ut)P gives p = P. Its time derivative is −uP. Add that term to the old free-cart Hamiltonian. The result produces the velocity measured from the moving origin.

example.title: A Hamiltonian in moving coordinates
steps: Use m = 1 kg, P = 3 kg·m/s and u = 2 m/s.
K = 3²/2 − 2 × 3 = −1.5 J. This K is not the ground-frame kinetic energy.

lessons.terms: u: The constant velocity of the translating origin. ∂F₂/∂t: The direct time derivative at fixed q and P. K: The Hamiltonian generating motion of Q and P.

lessons.title: Read momentum from an action function
lessons.idea: The position slope of Hamilton’s principal function gives momentum.
body: Hamilton’s principal function S assigns an action value to position and time for a chosen family of motion. Its partial derivative with position gives the paired momentum. The time input is held fixed. This is the same derivative rule used for a generating function.

equationGuide.meaning: Hamilton’s principal function S assigns an action value to position and time for a chosen family of motion. Its partial derivative with position gives the paired momentum. The time input is held fixed. This is the same derivative rule used for a generating function.

example.title: Read one momentum slope
steps: Take S(q, t) = (3 kg·m/s)q − (4 J)t.
At fixed time, its position derivative is p = 3 kg·m/s.

lessons.limits: The slope rule alone does not make an arbitrary function a solution. S must also satisfy the Hamilton–Jacobi equation for the chosen H. The displayed function is used only to read its momentum slope.

lessons.idea: The Hamilton–Jacobi equation connects the action’s time slope to the Hamiltonian.

lessons.title: Separate time when the Hamiltonian does not depend on it
lessons.idea: A time-independent Hamiltonian allows a useful action form S = W − Et.
body: Try S(q, t) = W(q) − Et, where E is a constant energy. The time derivative is −E. The Hamilton–Jacobi equation then becomes a position equation for W. For a particle with H = p²/(2m) + V(q), the rule below follows.

example.title: Find a momentum branch
steps: At a position where V = 0, use m = 2 kg and E = 4 J. Choose the positive-momentum branch.
dW/dq = +√(2m(E − V)) = 4 kg·m/s.

lessons.title: Recover a path from the action function
lessons.idea: Differentiating a complete action family with respect to its parameter recovers the path.
body: For a free cart, use S = Pq − P²t/(2m). The generating-function rule gives Q = ∂S/∂P = q − Pt/m. Here P and Q are constants because the transformed Hamiltonian is zero. Rearranging gives the familiar constant-velocity path; Q is the starting position at t = 0.

equationGuide.meaning: For a free cart, use S = Pq − P²t/(2m). The generating-function rule gives Q = ∂S/∂P = q − Pt/m. Here P and Q are constants because the transformed Hamiltonian is zero. Rearranging gives the familiar constant-velocity path; Q is the starting position at t = 0.

example.title: Recover one free-cart motion
steps: Use Q = 1 m, P = 4 kg·m/s and m = 2 kg.

lessons.terms: Complete action family: A solution containing enough independent constants to describe the allowed trajectories. Q: The constant starting position in this example. P: The constant momentum labeling the free-cart trajectory.

glossary.definition: A solution containing enough independent constants to describe the allowed trajectories.
The constant starting position in this example.

lessons.limits: This explicit recovery uses the free-particle Hamiltonian and its locally valid complete action family. More complex potentials may require integrals and separate action branches; the free-cart formula is not a general force law.

focus.idea: Differentiating a complete action family with respect to its parameter recovers the path.

lessons.title: Let neighbouring layers slow each other

lessons.title: Follow one small piece of fluid
lessons.idea: A fluid parcel moves with the flow where it is.
body: The velocity field describes places; a path describes one parcel. To find a path, keep evaluating the field at the parcel’s changing position. Adding velocity times a short time step estimates its next position; smaller steps improve this approximation when the velocity varies smoothly. equationGuide.meaning: A fluid parcel is a small piece of fluid that we follow. Its position is xₚ. Its velocity comes from the flow at that position, not from a fixed point elsewhere. In one direction, the rate of change of xₚ equals the local flow velocity u.

steps: A parcel starts at xₚ = 1 m. The flow everywhere stays at 2 m/s to the right.

body: The partial derivative holds x fixed because the meter does not travel. Different meters can report different time rates. A parcel generally passes several meters, so their spatial differences also affect its experience. This is why a fixed meter’s rate is not the whole parcel acceleration.

lessons.title: Draw a line along the flow arrows
lessons.idea: A streamline points along the flow at one instant.
body: A tiny step along a streamline must point along the local velocity. Its horizontal and vertical steps therefore have the ratio u:v. body: For rotation like a solid wheel with angular rate Ω, u = −Ωy and v = Ωx. The two cross-rates add to give ω_z = 2Ω. This factor of two is why vorticity is not itself the local angular speed. A general fluid element may stretch or shear while it turns.

lessons.title: Count only the flow through a surface

body: In a short time Δt, fluid crosses a uniform patch by the normal distance vₙΔt. Multiplying by area gives the signed swept volume; multiplying by density gives signed mass. Dividing by Δt gives ρAvₙ. Motion along the patch adds no swept volume through that patch.

lessons.title: Apply mass conservation at one place
lessons.idea: A local excess of outward mass flow lowers density.
body: Consider two faces of a small fixed interval. The difference in ρu between its right and left faces is the net outward mass rate per area. Dividing by the interval length gives ∂(ρu)/∂x. The minus sign converts net outward transport into the density change inside.

lessons.title: Connect spreading with a parcel’s density
lessons.idea: A parcel becomes less dense when it expands.
body: A small material parcel has mass ρV, where V is its volume. Its mass stays fixed, so V Dρ/Dt + ρ DV/Dt = 0. Local volume change satisfies (1/V)DV/Dt = ∇·v. Substituting gives Dρ/Dt = −ρ∇·v. This follows a moving volume, unlike the earlier fixed-region balance.

equationGuide.meaning: Follow a parcel without losing any of its mass. If its volume grows, that mass spreads out and density falls. The divergence ∇·v measures the local rate of volume spreading. Multiplying it by −ρ gives the density change while following the parcel.

example.title: An expanding parcel
steps: A parcel has density ρ = 4 kg/m³. The local divergence is 0.5 s⁻¹.

lessons.title: Keep a moving parcel’s volume unchanged
lessons.idea: Incompressible flow has zero local volume spreading.
body: With nonzero density, the parcel mass balance shows that Dρ/Dt = 0 requires ∇·v = 0. The individual spatial rates need not vanish. Their sum vanishes, so stretching in some directions is balanced by compression in others. This allows fluid to deform and accelerate without changing parcel volume.

equationGuide.meaning: In an incompressible model, a moving parcel keeps its volume and density. It can still stretch in one direction if it shrinks in another. The spatial velocity rates must add to zero. This does not mean the fluid is still or that its speed is the same everywhere.

example.title: Stretch one way and squeeze another
steps: In a flat incompressible flow, ∂u/∂x = 2 s⁻¹ and there is no z contribution.
Then ∂v/∂y = −2 s⁻¹, so the sum is zero.

lessons.title: Match the fluid velocity to a solid wall

body: A boundary condition tells a flow solution what must happen at an edge. No slip fixes the velocity at a solid wall; it does not choose the full profile inside. The interior still has to satisfy the force and mass balances. A moving wall can supply energy to the fluid through viscous stress.

equationGuide.meaning: For many ordinary liquid flows, the fluid right at a solid surface has the same velocity as the surface. This is called no slip. A still wall makes the touching fluid still. It does not make the fluid farther away still.

lessons.title: Use the local change between layers

body: The earlier plate formula used a straight velocity profile, so its slope was Δu/h everywhere. The local derivative ∂u/∂y lets the slope vary from one layer to the next. The shear stress component is τ_xy = 0.2 × 5 = 1 Pa.

lessons.title: Compare viscosity with density
lessons.idea: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density.
body: Dynamic viscosity sets stress for a given deformation rate. Density sets how much mass is being accelerated in a given volume. Dividing μ by ρ puts these roles together in the viscous acceleration term. Its units reduce to m²/s, which is why ν can set a spreading length squared per unit time.

equationGuide.meaning: The same stress changes the motion of a lighter parcel more easily. To compare viscous effects with the fluid’s mass, divide dynamic viscosity μ by density ρ. The result is kinematic viscosity ν. It helps set how quickly changes in motion spread through a fluid.

example.title: Divide by the density
steps: Use μ = 0.4 Pa·s and ρ = 800 kg/m³.

lessons.title: Estimate how long motion takes to spread
lessons.idea: Viscous spreading over a wider gap takes longer.

lessons.title: Find the total flow through a round pipe
lessons.idea: Laminar pipe flow is strongly affected by the pipe radius.
body: Thin rings in a pipe cross-section have area 2πr dr. Adding u(r) times those ring areas from r = 0 to R gives Q = πR⁴Δp/(8μL). The average speed is half the centre speed for this profile. Continuity still holds: the same total Q passes each slice of the steady pipe.

equationGuide.meaning: Add the flow through every small part of the pipe’s cross-section. For the parabolic laminar profile, this gives Poiseuille’s law. steps: A pipe carries Q = 0.001 m³/s. We double its radius while keeping Δp, μ and L fixed, and the flow stays laminar.

lessons.idea: A pressure difference pushes fluid toward lower pressure.
body: For a small box of width Δx and face area A, the net pressure force along x is approximately −(∂p/∂x)Δx A. The box volume is Δx A. Dividing force by volume leaves −∂p/∂x. Equal pressure contributions cancel before taking the small-box limit.

lessons.title: Balance pressure and gravity with acceleration
lessons.idea: Without viscosity, pressure and gravity set parcel acceleration.
body: The parcel’s mass is ρ times its volume. Newton’s rule says this mass times its material acceleration equals the sum of forces. Divide by volume to compare pressure force −∂p/∂x and gravity force ρgₓ. Dividing again by density gives the acceleration equation shown here.

equationGuide.meaning: Newton’s force rule also works for a fluid parcel. Divide the pressure force per volume by density to get its acceleration contribution. Add the gravity component gₓ. This is the x component of Euler’s fluid equation, which neglects viscous forces.

lessons.title: Balance pressure with gravity in still fluid
lessons.idea: Still fluid needs a pressure gradient to support its weight.
body: For a still parcel, the upward pressure-force density is −dp/dz and the downward weight-force density is −ρg. Their sum must be zero. Thus dp/dz = −ρg. If ρ is constant, integrating over a height change gives Δp = −ρgΔz, matching the familiar pressure-with-depth rule.

equationGuide.meaning: Choose z to point upward and let g be the positive size of gravity. In still fluid, acceleration is zero. The upward pressure force must balance the downward weight. Pressure therefore falls as height increases. This force balance is called hydrostatic balance.

example.title: Pressure falls upward
steps: A still liquid has density 1000 kg/m³. Use g = 10 m/s².

lessons.title: Keep an energy balance along an ideal streamline
lessons.idea: In ideal steady flow, pressure, motion and height share an energy balance.
body: Along a steady inviscid streamline, the pressure force supplies changes in kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy. For constant density, integrating the force rule along the path gives p/ρ + v²/2 + gz = a constant. Multiplying by ρ gives the displayed energy-per-volume form. Viscous dissipation changes this mechanical-energy balance.
lessons.equation: p + ½ρv² + ρgz = constant along one streamline

equationGuide.meaning: For steady flow with constant density and negligible viscosity, follow one streamline. Pressure p, motion energy per volume ρv²/2, and height energy per volume ρgz add to a constant. This is Bernoulli’s rule. At the same height, gaining speed uses some of the pressure contribution.

example.title: Speed rises at the same height
steps: Take ρ = 2 kg/m³. Speed rises from 1 to 3 m/s along a horizontal streamline.
The motion term rises by ½ × 2 × (9 − 1) = 8 Pa, so pressure falls by 8 Pa.

lessons.title: Find the local acceleration caused by viscosity
lessons.idea: Viscous acceleration depends on the bend of the velocity profile.
body: In simple shear, τ_xy = μ∂u/∂y. The difference in shear stress across a small fluid piece gives a force per volume ∂τ_xy/∂y. With constant μ this is μ∂²u/∂y². Divide by density to get ν∂²u/∂y². The net force depends on a stress difference, not on stress at just one side.

equationGuide.meaning: In simple shear, neighbouring layers pull on a thin fluid piece from opposite sides. If the shear stress changes across it, the pulls do not cancel. For constant viscosity and density, the viscous contribution to acceleration is ν times the second spatial derivative of u. This derivative measures the profile’s bend.

example.title: A downward-bending profile
steps: Use ν = 0.1 m²/s and ∂²u/∂y² = −6 (m/s)/m².
The viscous contribution is 0.1 × (−6) = −0.6 m/s².

lessons.terms: ∂²u/∂y²: How the velocity slope changes across y; the profile’s curvature. ν: Kinematic viscosity. Viscous contribution: The part of acceleration produced by viscous forces, before adding other forces.

glossary.definition: How the velocity slope changes across y; the profile’s curvature.

lessons.limits: This expression is for simple shear u(y), with constant μ and ρ. A straight profile can have nonzero shear stress but zero net viscous force on each interior piece. Other forces may balance a nonzero viscous contribution.

lessons.title: Put the fluid force terms together
lessons.idea: Navier–Stokes adds viscous forces to the parcel’s force balance.
body: The pressure, gravity and viscous contributions are all forces per mass. Adding them follows Newton’s rule for the same parcel. In incompressible constant-viscosity flow, the viscous contribution becomes ν times the Laplacian of each velocity component. The material acceleration on the left still includes advection, so the equation is generally nonlinear.

equationGuide.meaning: For an incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant density and viscosity, add three acceleration contributions: pressure, viscosity and gravity. Their sum gives the parcel’s acceleration. The symbol ∇²u adds the bends of the x velocity across all three directions. This is the x part of the Navier–Stokes equation.

example.title: Three contributions at one point
steps: The pressure, viscous and gravity contributions are +4, −1 and 0 m/s².
The parcel’s x acceleration is 4 − 1 + 0 = 3 m/s².

lessons.title: Find the force needed to change a stream’s momentum
lessons.idea: A steady change in momentum flow needs a net force.
body: Mass leaving the region takes its x momentum with it, while incoming mass brings x momentum in. With no change in the stored momentum, the net external force supplies the difference between those transport rates. For uniform inlet and outlet velocities the rates are ṁu_in and ṁu_out. A bend requires the same balance separately for each direction.

equationGuide.meaning: Choose a fixed region with one inlet and one outlet. If no momentum builds up inside, the net force on the fluid equals momentum carried out per second minus momentum carried in per second. For uniform flow at each opening, use the common mass flow rate times the change in a velocity component.

example.title: A stream speeds up
steps: The mass flow is 3 kg/s. The x velocity changes from 1 m/s at the inlet to 5 m/s at the outlet.
The net x force on the fluid is 3 × (5 − 1) = 12 N.

lessons.terms: Momentum flow: Momentum carried through a boundary per second. ṁ: Mass flow rate, in kilograms per second. u_in and u_out: Signed x velocity components at the inlet and outlet. Net force: The sum of pressure, wall and body forces on the chosen fluid.

For nonuniform profiles, integrate momentum flux rather than multiplying arbitrary averages. The reaction force exerted by the fluid on a wall has the opposite sign to the wall’s force on the fluid; pressure forces must also be counted.

lessons.title: Compare motion with viscous effects
lessons.idea: The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity at chosen scales.
body: A convective acceleration has typical size U²/L. A viscous acceleration has typical size νU/L². Their ratio is UL/ν. This comparison explains the Reynolds number without asserting that every term has exactly that size everywhere. Near a wall, velocity may change across a much smaller length than L.

equationGuide.meaning: Choose a typical speed U and length L for the flow. Divide UL by kinematic viscosity ν. This gives the Reynolds number Re, a number with no units. A small Re means viscosity is strong compared with inertia on those scales. A large Re means inertia matters more, but viscosity can still matter near walls.

steps: Use U = 0.02 m/s, L = 0.01 m and ν = 0.001 m²/s.

lessons.title: Match the balance of effects in a scale model
lessons.idea: Matching Reynolds numbers matches one important flow balance.
body: For the constant-property incompressible momentum equation, scaling distance by L and velocity by U gives a viscous coefficient 1/Re. Matching Re can therefore make the dimensionless equations match for corresponding setups. The conclusion also requires matching shape and conditions. Additional physics can add coefficients that Re does not control.

equationGuide.meaning: A small model can help study a larger flow. If the shapes are scaled copies, matching Re keeps the same inertia-to-viscosity comparison. In the same fluid, shrinking the model requires a larger speed to keep UL unchanged. Other effects may need their own matching rules.

steps: The full object has L = 2 m and U = 3 m/s. The model has L = 1 m in the same fluid.
The matching model speed is 3 × 2 ÷ 1 = 6 m/s.

lessons.title: Compare flow speed with sound speed
lessons.idea: The Mach number compares a flow speed with the local sound speed.
body: A disturbance crosses length L in time L/c, while the flow travels that length in time L/U. Their ratio is U/c. At small Ma, pressure information can cross the region much faster than fluid travels through it. This helps explain the low-speed approximation, while leaving thermal and composition changes as separate density effects.

equationGuide.meaning: Sound carries small pressure disturbances through a fluid. Divide flow speed U by the local sound speed c to get the Mach number Ma. When this ratio is small, density changes caused by the motion are often small too. Strong heating can still change density, even in a slow flow.

example.title: A flow much slower than sound
steps: Take U = 30 m/s and c = 300 m/s.

lessons.terms: Mach number, Ma: Flow speed divided by local sound speed. c: The local speed of small sound disturbances relative to the fluid. Compressibility: The ability of a fluid’s density to change under pressure.

lessons.limits: Use U relative to the chosen object or flow frame and c at the local thermodynamic state. lessons.title: Estimate how far a wall’s influence spreads
lessons.idea: A wall affects a thin layer of a fast passing flow.
body: A parcel reaches distance x in a time of order x/U. Viscosity spreads its influence over a distance of order √(νt). Substituting the travel time gives √(νx/U). The estimate assumes a thin attached laminar layer; an exact edge requires a chosen velocity threshold and a more detailed solution.

equationGuide.meaning: The boundary layer is the region where velocity changes from the wall value toward the outer flow. Along a flat plate, fluid has about x/U seconds to feel viscosity. The laminar thickness scale therefore grows like the square root of νx/U. This is a size estimate, not an exact measured edge.

example.title: Farther along a plate
steps: Use ν = 0.0001 m²/s, x = 1 m and U = 1 m/s.
The thickness scale is √0.0001 = 0.01 m.

lessons.title: Use wall shear to detect nearby flow reversal
lessons.idea: A reversed velocity slope at a wall signals nearby reverse flow.
body: Near a still no-slip wall, a smooth velocity profile starts as u(y) approximately equal to y times its wall slope. This makes the slope’s sign a local indicator of forward or reversed flow. Pressure rising downstream can slow near-wall fluid enough to reverse it. Identifying separation requires the surrounding flow as well as this local indicator.

equationGuide.meaning: Take x along the outer flow and y away from a still wall. The velocity at the wall is zero. A positive wall slope means the nearby fluid moves forward; a negative slope means it moves backward. Wall shear tracks this slope. In steady flat two-dimensional flow, a change through zero can mark separation, where flow leaves the wall region.

example.title: A reversed near-wall slope
steps: Use μ = 0.1 Pa·s and a wall slope of −2 s⁻¹.
τ_w = −0.2 Pa. The negative slope shows nearby reverse flow.

lessons.terms: τ_w: Signed tangential force per area exerted by the fluid on the wall, positive along x. Separation: Flow moving away from the wall region, often with nearby reverse flow. Wall slope: The spatial velocity rate just outside the wall.

lessons.title: Describe drag with a dimensionless number
lessons.idea: A drag coefficient compares drag with a chosen flow-force scale.
body: The quantity ρU²/2 is a pressure scale, often called dynamic pressure. Multiplying it by a reference area gives a force scale. C_D is the actual drag divided by that force scale. Stating the area and the flow conditions makes the comparison reproducible; changing either can change the reported coefficient.

equationGuide.meaning: Drag is the force component opposing motion through a fluid. To compare objects and flow conditions, write its magnitude using density ρ, speed U, reference area A and a drag coefficient C_D. The coefficient must come from a suitable measurement or model. It is not the same number for every speed or shape.

example.title: Use a known drag coefficient
steps: For stated flow conditions, use ρ = 2 kg/m³, U = 3 m/s, A = 1 m² and C_D = 0.5.

lessons.terms: Drag, F_D: The magnitude of the force component opposing relative motion. C_D: Dimensionless drag coefficient for specified conditions and area choice. A: The chosen reference area, which must be stated. U: Relative flow speed away from the disturbed region.

glossary.definition: The magnitude of the force component opposing relative motion.
Dimensionless drag coefficient for specified conditions and area choice.
The chosen reference area, which must be stated.
Relative flow speed away from the disturbed region.

lessons.limits: C_D can depend on Reynolds number, Mach number, shape, surface roughness and the chosen area. The formula is a definition or comparison rule, not a universal prediction that drag always scales as U². Creeping-flow C_D, for example, changes with U.

lessons.title: Separate the average flow from its changes
lessons.idea: An instantaneous velocity can be split into a mean and a fluctuation.
body: Subtracting the same sample mean from each equally weighted reading makes those fluctuations average to zero. Their individual values can still be large. In a statistically steady flow, a suitable mean can stay fixed while the instantaneous velocity changes. A short record may not represent the longer-term statistics.

equationGuide.meaning: At one place, a turbulent flow has irregular velocity changes. Choose an averaging method and call the mean velocity ū. The fluctuation u′ is the current reading minus that mean. This split describes the changes, but a changing reading alone does not prove turbulence; an orderly oscillation changes too.

example.title: A reading above the mean
steps: The mean at a point is ū = 5 m/s. One reading is u = 7 m/s.
That reading has fluctuation u′ = 7 − 5 = 2 m/s.

lessons.terms: Mean, ū: Velocity averaged over a stated time window or set of repeated samples. Fluctuation, u′: The difference between a reading and that mean. Turbulent flow: Flow with irregular interacting motions across many sizes.

glossary.definition: Velocity averaged over a stated time window or set of repeated samples.
The difference between a reading and that mean.
Flow with irregular interacting motions across many sizes.

lessons.limits: State the averaging method and choose an interval appropriate to the question. A finite average can miss slow changes. This algebraic split works for laminar unsteady flows too and is not a test that establishes turbulence.

focus.idea: An instantaneous velocity can be split into a mean and a fluctuation.

steps: The mean at a point is ū = 5 m/s. One reading is u = 7 m/s.

lessons.title: Measure the typical size of velocity changes
lessons.idea: Squaring fluctuations prevents opposite signs from cancelling.
body: A signed average answers whether changes favour one direction. Averaging squared fluctuations instead answers how large they typically are. Taking the square root returns to velocity units. RMS is nonnegative and remains positive for equal positive and negative fluctuations unless every fluctuation is zero.

equationGuide.meaning: Positive and negative fluctuations can average to zero even when the flow changes strongly. To measure their typical size, square them, average the squares, then take the square root. This is the root-mean-square fluctuation, u_rms. It has the same units as velocity.

example.title: Two opposite fluctuations
steps: Two equally weighted fluctuations are +2 and −2 m/s. Their squared values are both 4 m²/s².

lessons.terms: Root-mean-square, rms: Square, average, then take the square root. u_rms: Typical fluctuation size for one velocity component. Equally weighted: Each sample contributes the same amount to the average.

glossary.definition: Square, average, then take the square root.
Typical fluctuation size for one velocity component.
Each sample contributes the same amount to the average.

lessons.limits: Use the same mean and averaging procedure as in the fluctuation definition. Two readings illustrate the arithmetic; they are not enough to characterize a real turbulent flow. RMS measures size, not direction or the full distribution.

lessons.title: Track momentum carried by velocity fluctuations
lessons.idea: Linked velocity fluctuations can transport momentum across a flow.
body: Multiplying u = ū + u′ and v = v̄ + v′ and averaging leaves ūv̄ plus mean(u′v′), when the fluctuations have zero mean. That extra product transports momentum in the averaged equation. Two zero individual means do not imply a zero product mean. A closure model estimates this missing information but brings its own assumptions.

equationGuide.meaning: A sideways-moving fluid piece can carry extra forward momentum with it. To describe this in a constant-density averaged flow, multiply its forward fluctuation u′ by its sideways fluctuation v′, then average. The stress-like term −ρ times this average is called Reynolds shear stress. Averaging does not remove this effect.

example.title: Fluctuations move together
steps: Use ρ = 2 kg/m³ and mean(u′v′) = −0.5 m²/s².

lessons.terms: Reynolds shear stress: A stress-like term representing momentum transport by correlated velocity fluctuations. u′ and v′: Fluctuations along x and y. Correlated: Tending to vary together rather than independently. ρ: Constant fluid density in this formula.

glossary.definition: A stress-like term representing momentum transport by correlated velocity fluctuations.
Fluctuations along x and y.
Tending to vary together rather than independently.
Constant fluid density in this formula.

lessons.limits: This sign convention places −ρ mean(u′v′) with stress terms in the averaged momentum equation. It is not molecular viscosity. Predicting it requires fluctuation data or a turbulence model; the mean velocity alone does not close the equations. Variable-density flows require more careful averaging.

lessons.title: Separate charged parts from net charge
lessons.idea: A plasma can contain many charged particles while having nearly zero net charge.
body: A plasma contains free charged particles that can respond together to electric fields. Electrons carry negative charge. Here each ion carries one equal positive charge. Almost equal numbers can nearly cancel overall, even though the individual particles remain charged.
lessons.equation: net charge = e × (number of ions − number of electrons)

steps: A region contains 1001 singly charged positive ions and 1000 electrons.
The net charge is +e: just one elementary charge, despite 2001 charged particles.

lessons.title: Find how shielding length changes
lessons.idea: Debye length gives a distance scale for electric shielding in a plasma.
body: Mobile charges rearrange around an electric disturbance and weaken its field. At fixed electron temperature, four times the electron density makes the electron Debye length half as large. More electrons in the same space can screen the disturbance over a shorter distance.

In the full electron expression below, ε₀ is vacuum permittivity, k_B is Boltzmann’s constant, T_e is electron temperature in kelvin, n_e is electron number density and e is elementary charge. The lesson compares two cases so the unchanged constants cancel.

equationGuide.meaning: Mobile charges rearrange around an electric disturbance and weaken its field. At fixed electron temperature, four times the electron density makes the electron Debye length half as large. More electrons in the same space can screen the disturbance over a shorter distance.

example.title: A denser plasma
steps: The electron Debye length starts at 6 mm. Increase electron density by a factor of 4 without changing temperature.
The length becomes 6 ÷ √4 = 3 mm.

lessons.title: Let displaced electrons swing back
lessons.idea: A displaced electron cloud can oscillate against the positive charge left behind.
body: Move electrons slightly away from their balanced positions. The resulting electric field pulls them back. They can pass the balance point and swing again. In the simple cold-electron model, four times the electron density gives twice the angular oscillation frequency.

In the full expression below, n_e is electron number density, e is elementary charge, m_e is electron mass and ε₀ is vacuum permittivity. Ordinary frequency in cycles per second is the angular frequency divided by two pi.

equationGuide.meaning: Move electrons slightly away from their balanced positions. The resulting electric field pulls them back. They can pass the balance point and swing again. In the simple cold-electron model, four times the electron density gives twice the angular oscillation frequency.

example.title: Change the density
steps: An electron plasma oscillation has angular frequency 2 million rad/s. Make the electron density 4 times larger.
The new angular frequency is 2 × √4 = 4 million rad/s.

lessons.terms: Angular frequency (ω): The rate a cycle’s phase changes, in radians per second. Electron plasma oscillation: A collective back-and-forth motion of electrons against positive background charge.

glossary.definition: The rate a cycle’s phase changes, in radians per second.

lessons.limits: This simple frequency assumes small displacements, immobile ions, negligible collisions and an unmagnetized cold-electron model. Warm plasma waves can also depend on wavelength.

focus.explanation: Move electrons slightly away from their balanced positions. The resulting electric field pulls them back. They can pass the balance point and swing again. In the simple cold-electron model, four times the electron density gives twice the angular oscillation frequency.

steps: An electron plasma oscillation has angular frequency 2 million rad/s. Make the electron density 4 times larger.

lessons.title: Read the extra decay caused by shielding
lessons.idea: A plasma makes a weak charge’s electric effect fade faster with distance.
body: The 1/r factor is already present for an isolated charge in empty space. Comparing at equal r cancels that factor and isolates the effect of plasma screening. Comparing two different radii must retain both factors.

steps: At r = 2λ_D, the screening factor is exp(−2) ≈ 0.135.

body: In a frame moving at v_E, the perpendicular electric force is cancelled by the magnetic force q v_E × B. The remaining perpendicular motion is gyromotion. Charge cancels from the drift balance, explaining the common direction.

lessons.title: Track perpendicular energy in a slowly changing field
lessons.idea: The perpendicular energy divided by field strength can stay nearly constant.
body: Conservation of μ_m makes K_perp proportional to B. In a static magnetic field without electric forces, total kinetic energy also stays fixed. The parallel part must therefore decrease as the perpendicular part grows.

equationGuide.meaning: When the field changes gently over an orbit, the particle’s magnetic moment μ_m is approximately conserved. It equals perpendicular kinetic energy K_perp divided by B. lessons.title: Balance forces on one plasma species
lessons.idea: Fields and pressure can change a group of particles’ average motion.
body: Averaging particle forces gives a force per volume. Dividing by m_s n_s converts it to mean acceleration. Random velocity spread supplies pressure; it is not the same as mean directed motion. A full model also needs a rule for pressure and consistent field equations.

equationGuide.meaning: A plasma fluid equation follows the average motion of one species. The Lorentz force comes from electric and magnetic fields. lessons.title: Let different species carry a current
lessons.idea: Balanced charge can still carry current.
body: The general current is the sum of charge times number density times mean velocity over species. With charges +e and −e and equal n, this becomes the displayed difference. Charge neutrality constrains densities, not the equality of their velocities.

lessons.title: Relate the electric field to a moving magnetic fluid
lessons.idea: Ideal MHD sets the electric field to zero in the moving fluid frame.
body: The ideal rule, combined with Faraday’s law, leads to magnetic flux conservation through a surface moving with the fluid. That statement needs smooth solutions and the ideal approximation. Real reconnection requires physics beyond this simple rule.

equationGuide.meaning: Magnetohydrodynamics, or MHD, treats plasma as a conducting fluid. In its ideal limit, the electric field balances the magnetic part of the force on a charge moving with the fluid. This gives E = −u × B. It is an approximation with important scale limits.

example.title: Perpendicular flow and field
steps: The bulk speed is 3 m/s perpendicular to a field of 2 T.
The ideal electric-field magnitude is UB = 6 V/m.

lessons.terms: MHD: A large-scale model of a conducting fluid and magnetic field. Ideal limit: A model neglecting resistive and several small-scale terms. u: Bulk fluid velocity.

glossary.definition: A large-scale model of a conducting fluid and magnetic field.

lessons.limits: Large-scale, low-frequency single-fluid approximation with negligible resistivity, Hall and electron-inertia effects. It is not a universal property of every plasma or every scale.

lessons.title: Compare magnetic pressure with fluid pressure
lessons.idea: A magnetic field contributes a pressure scale proportional to B squared.
body: For a straight field tangent to parallel layers in static balance, p + B²/(2μ₀) can be constant across the layers. More general geometry also includes a force along field curvature. The pressure-to-magnetic-pressure ratio is often called plasma beta.

equationGuide.meaning: Magnetic energy per volume has the same units as pressure. Its value B²/(2μ₀) is called magnetic pressure. It can help balance plasma pressure. A curved field also has a tension effect, so magnetic pressure alone does not describe every magnetic force.

example.title: Double the field
steps: A magnetic field has pressure scale p_B = 5 Pa. Double its magnitude.
The new magnetic pressure is 4 × 5 = 20 Pa.

lessons.terms: p_B: Magnetic pressure, in pascals. μ₀: Vacuum permeability. Magnetic tension: The directional force associated with bending magnetic field lines.

glossary.definition: Magnetic pressure, in pascals.
Vacuum permeability.

lessons.limits: The pressure scale is general, but treating it as the entire magnetic force is not. The simple total-pressure balance needs a static planar geometry with the stated field orientation.

lessons.title: Write the restoring rule for an electron cloud
lessons.idea: A small electron displacement creates a restoring electric force.
body: Gauss’s law links the displacement to the charge-separation field. The electron force then gives an acceleration proportional to −x. The minus sign restores the balanced position; inertia carries the cloud past it.

equationGuide.meaning: In a simple unmagnetized model, ions stay still while electrons shift slightly. Charge separation creates an electric field that pulls the electrons back. Their displacement x follows the same form as a spring oscillator, with electron plasma frequency ω_pe.

example.title: A restoring acceleration
steps: Use ω_pe = 3 rad/s and x = 0.02 m.
The acceleration is −9 × 0.02 = −0.18 m/s².

lessons.terms: ω_pe: Electron plasma angular frequency, √(n_e e²/(ε₀m_e)). x: Small displacement from charge balance.

glossary.definition: Electron plasma angular frequency, √(n_e e²/(ε₀m_e)).
Small displacement from charge balance.

lessons.limits: Linear cold-electron model with fixed ions, negligible collisions and no background magnetic field. This is a collective disturbance, not the circular gyrofrequency.

lessons.title: Let thermal motion change the wave frequency
lessons.idea: Random electron motion changes a wave’s frequency.
body: This is the Bohm–Gross approximation. The pressure term makes the wave dispersive: frequency changes with k. Its derivation assumes phase speed high compared with the thermal speed; using the equation outside that regime can miss strong kinetic damping.

equationGuide.meaning: Thermal motion adds a pressure response to the electron oscillation. In a long-wavelength approximation for Maxwellian electrons, the frequency includes a term with wavenumber k. Shorter wavelengths have larger k. Define v_te as √(k_B T_e/m_e); this convention fixes the factor 3.

example.title: Add the thermal contribution
steps: Use ω_pe = 100 rad/s, k = 1 m⁻¹ and v_te = 1 m/s. Here kλ_De = 0.01, within the long-wavelength limit.
The squared frequency is ω² ≈ 10000 + 3 = 10003 s⁻².

lessons.terms: k: Wavenumber, 2π divided by wavelength. v_te: One-component thermal speed √(k_B T_e/m_e). Maxwellian: The equilibrium thermal velocity distribution.

glossary.definition: Wavenumber, 2π divided by wavelength.
One-component thermal speed √(k_B T_e/m_e).
The equilibrium thermal velocity distribution.

lessons.limits: Small-amplitude unmagnetized electron waves, immobile ions, kλ_De much smaller than one and weak damping. Higher-order thermal terms and kinetic damping are omitted.

focus.idea: Random electron motion changes a wave’s frequency.
focus.explanation: In this model, electrons have a bell-shaped spread of velocities and the wavelength is long. Their random motion adds a pressure effect. The wave then depends on k, the wave number: a larger k means a shorter wavelength. Here v_te means √(k_B T_e/m_e). This definition sets the factor 3 in the equation.

example.title: Add the thermal contribution
steps: Use ω_pe = 100 rad/s, k = 1 m⁻¹ and v_te = 1 m/s. Here kλ_De = 0.01, within the long-wavelength limit.

lessons.title: Check whether a transverse wave can travel
lessons.idea: Some low-frequency waves fade inside a plasma instead of traveling through it.
body: Solving for k² gives (ω²−ω_pe²)/c². Its sign distinguishes propagating and evanescent solutions. Interfaces, finite thickness and collisions affect reflection, penetration and absorption; the bulk dispersion alone does not settle all of those.

equationGuide.meaning: For a simple transverse electromagnetic wave, the frequency must exceed the electron plasma frequency to give a real nonzero k. Below that cutoff, k is imaginary and the field is evanescent: it decays with distance instead of forming a travelling bulk wave.

example.title: Below the cutoff
steps: The plasma frequency is 10 million rad/s and the applied wave frequency is 8 million rad/s.
Then c²k² = ω² − ω_pe² is negative, so the bulk field is evanescent.

lessons.terms: c: Speed of light in vacuum. Evanescent: Decaying in space rather than propagating as a bulk travelling wave. Cutoff: A frequency boundary for propagation in this model.

glossary.definition: Speed of light in vacuum.
Decaying in space rather than propagating as a bulk travelling wave.
A frequency boundary for propagation in this model.

lessons.limits: Cold, collisionless, uniform, unmagnetized plasma with effectively immobile ions for this high-frequency transverse mode. Magnetized modes have different cutoffs.

focus.idea: Some low-frequency waves fade inside a plasma instead of traveling through it.
focus.explanation: Use the simple cold-plasma model with no background magnetic field. A traveling electromagnetic wave needs a frequency above the electron plasma frequency. Below that boundary, the field fades with distance. This fading pattern is called evanescent.

example.title: Below the cutoff
steps: The plasma frequency is 10 million rad/s and the applied wave frequency is 8 million rad/s.

lessons.title: Find a simple ion-acoustic speed
lessons.idea: Electron pressure can push ions back and forth to make a wave.
body: Ion acceleration is driven by the electric field arising from the electron pressure response. Combining ion momentum and continuity with quasineutrality produces the wave equation. Warm ions add pressure terms and kinetic damping can become important.

equationGuide.meaning: In an ion-acoustic wave, ions provide most of the moving mass. Warm electrons supply much of the restoring pressure. With cold singly charged ions and isothermal electrons, the long-wavelength sound speed is √(k_B T_e/m_i).

example.title: Heat the electrons
steps: Keep the ion species fixed and multiply electron temperature by 4. The old speed is 3 km/s.
The new speed is 3 × √4 = 6 km/s.

lessons.terms: Ion-acoustic wave: A low-frequency compressive wave involving ion motion and electron pressure. m_i: Mass of one ion. Isothermal electrons: An electron pressure response with fixed temperature.

glossary.definition: A low-frequency compressive wave involving ion motion and electron pressure.
Mass of one ion.
An electron pressure response with fixed temperature.

lessons.limits: Small-amplitude, long-wavelength, quasineutral mode with singly charged cold ions and much hotter electrons. This simple speed is not valid for arbitrary species temperatures.

focus.idea: Electron pressure can push ions back and forth to make a wave.
focus.explanation: In an ion-sound wave, ions provide most of the moving mass. Warm electrons provide much of the pressure pushing them back. The speed shown applies to long waves, cold ions with one positive charge each, and electrons kept at a fixed temperature.

lessons.title: Find the speed of a magnetic bending wave
lessons.idea: Magnetic tension restores an Alfvén wave.
body: A stronger field gives more tension and a faster restoring response. More mass gives more inertia and a slower response. In this ideal parallel-propagation limit the frequency is k_parallel v_A.

equationGuide.meaning: A small sideways bend of magnetic field lines pulls back through magnetic tension. The plasma’s mass resists that acceleration. In ideal MHD, a shear Alfvén wave travelling along the field has speed B divided by √(μ₀ρ), where ρ is mass density.

example.title: Increase mass density
steps: Keep B fixed and raise ρ by a factor of 4. The old Alfvén speed is 8 km/s.
The new speed is 8/2 = 4 km/s.

glossary.definition: A transverse magnetic-tension wave in a plasma.

lessons.title: Read whether a small disturbance grows
lessons.idea: The sign of a growth rate distinguishes growth from decay.
body: The mode convention exp[i(kx−ωt)] gives γ = Im(ω). A positive imaginary part grows with time in this convention. A test of one mode is not proof that all possible disturbances are stable; the background and allowed modes matter.

equationGuide.meaning: For a linear mode, write its amplitude as A₀ exp(γt). Positive γ means exponential growth, negative γ means decay, and zero γ means this factor stays constant. This tests one small disturbance in a specified model; it does not describe its final large-amplitude state.

example.title: A growing disturbance
steps: A mode has γ = ln(2) s⁻¹, so it doubles each second. Its starting amplitude is 0.01.
After 2 s its amplitude is 0.01 × 4 = 0.04.

lessons.terms: γ (gamma): Linear growth rate, in inverse seconds. ln(2): The natural logarithm of 2; exp(ln(2)) = 2. Linear stability: Behaviour of sufficiently small perturbations about a chosen state.

glossary.definition: Linear growth rate, in inverse seconds.
The natural logarithm of 2; exp(ln(2)) = 2.

lessons.limits: Linear stage only. Growing disturbances eventually invalidate the small-amplitude approximation. Stability conclusions require checking the relevant modes and boundary conditions.

lessons.title: Count particles by their velocities
lessons.idea: A velocity distribution tells us how particles are spread across velocities.
body: For a small interval Δv, the number density in it is approximately f(v)Δv. The full three-dimensional distribution is integrated over all three velocity components. A distribution can carry information that a single mean speed loses.

equationGuide.meaning: At a chosen place, f(v) describes how many particles occupy each small velocity range. Adding f(v) across all velocities gives number density n. This one-dimensional distribution has already included the other velocity directions. A peak means many particles have velocities near that value.

example.title: Add velocity groups
steps: Two non-overlapping velocity groups contribute number densities of 3 and 5 particles per m³.
The total density is 3 + 5 = 8 particles per m³.

lessons.terms: f(v): Number density per unit velocity interval. ∫ f(v) dv: The sum of contributions from all velocity intervals. Distribution: A description of how a quantity is spread over possible values.

lessons.title: Find the mean flow from a velocity distribution
lessons.idea: The mean velocity weights each group by how many particles it contains.
body: The integral sums momentum-related contributions from all velocity groups. A zero mean does not imply zero kinetic energy because energy depends on velocity squared. Mean flow is one moment of the distribution, not the whole distribution.

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply each velocity by its particle density, add the results, then divide by total density. This is the mean flow velocity u. Positive and negative velocities can cancel in the mean even when individual particles move quickly.

body: For one-dimensional electrostatic motion, the equation is ∂f/∂t + v∂f/∂x + (qE/m)∂f/∂v = 0. The last term accounts for acceleration through velocity space. Integrating velocity moments recovers fluid balances, but higher moments introduce a closure problem.

lessons.idea: Speed and collision rate tell us a typical travel distance between collisions.
body: The collision time scale is about 1/ν_c. Multiplying by typical speed gives a distance scale. Coulomb relaxation often accumulates many small deflections rather than a single hard collision, so the chosen effective rate must be stated.

lessons.title: Find particles that stay near a wave’s phase
lessons.idea: Particles near a wave’s phase speed can exchange energy with it for longer.
body: The sign and strength of the exchange depend on the distribution near resonance and on the mode. For the usual stable Maxwellian electron Langmuir mode, the wave loses energy. The resonance condition alone does not calculate a damping rate or prove stability.

equationGuide.meaning: A particle moving nearly alongside a wave crest keeps seeing a similar electric-field phase. In one dimension, resonance occurs near v = ω_r/k. This is central to Landau damping: a wave can transfer energy to particles without binary collisions. Other velocity distributions can instead feed energy into a wave.

example.title: Match a wave phase
steps: A wave has real frequency ω_r = 12 rad/s and k = 3 m⁻¹.
Its resonant velocity is 12/3 = 4 m/s.

lessons.title: Use the time a clock actually records
lessons.idea: Proper time is the time recorded by a clock along its own path.
body: A chosen time coordinate need not match a local clock. For a clock held at one place in a static spacetime, a factor A converts coordinate time into clock time. This is a local conversion; comparing two clocks needs both of their factors.

In the static metric below, c is the speed of light, dt is a tiny coordinate-time interval and dτ is a tiny interval of proper time. With no spatial motion, the metric gives the clock conversion. The factor A is held constant along this fixed clock’s path.

time part of metric: ds² = −A²c²dt²

lessons.title: Compare nearby freely falling objects
lessons.idea: In a small freely falling lab, nearby free objects can seem weightless.
body: If the lab and an object fall with the same acceleration, their relative acceleration is zero. A nearby observer in the lab does not see the object fall toward the floor. This local result is a starting point for the equivalence principle.

lessons.title: Read a clock’s time from its timelike interval
lessons.idea: A clock measures proper time along its own path.
body: For a curved or accelerating path, apply the infinitesimal rule to each small segment and integrate dτ. One cannot generally calculate the full elapsed time by applying a flat endpoint formula to a curved path.

lessons.title: Use the metric to lower a vector index
lessons.idea: The metric converts between two ways of writing a vector’s parts.
body: The metric performs a linear transformation on the component list. Lowering an index is not merely renaming it. Contractions such as A_μ A^μ give coordinate-independent scalars when the tensor rules are followed.

lessons.title: Allow coordinate directions to change

body: The angular metric entry is r². In the Levi-Civita connection, Γ^r_θθ = −½ ∂(r²)/∂r = −r. Cartesian coordinates on the same flat plane have zero connection coefficients.

lessons.title: Keep a vector parallel along a chosen path
lessons.idea: You can carry an arrow along a path without turning it locally.
body: The exact transport equation is dV^μ/dλ + Γ^μ_νρ (dx^ν/dλ)V^ρ = 0. Multiplying by a small parameter step gives the displayed estimate. In curved geometry, transporting along different paths can give different results.

example.title: A short transport step
steps: For one contributing term, use Γ = 0.2 m⁻¹, V = 5 and Δx = 0.01 m.

lessons.title: Write the equation for a free-fall path
lessons.idea: A freely falling object follows the straightest path allowed by spacetime.
body: Substitute the tangent vector into the parallel-transport equation. For massive free particles, proper time is an affine parameter and yields this form. Light follows null geodesics with another affine parameter because its proper-time interval is zero.

equationGuide.meaning: An ideal freely falling point particle follows a geodesic when no other force acts. Its tangent vector changes only as required by the geometry. In coordinates, that gives an acceleration term plus a connection term equal to zero. A coordinate acceleration can therefore be nonzero even in free fall.

example.title: A coordinate acceleration
steps: At a point, the only contribution to the chosen spatial equation has Γ = 0.5 m⁻¹ and dx/dτ = 2 m/s.
The coordinate acceleration is −0.5 × 2² = −2 m/s².

lessons.title: Measure how the order of geometric changes matters
lessons.idea: In curved geometry, changing the order of two steps can change the result.
body: Connection coefficients can be nonzero in flat coordinates, but their derivative and product contributions cancel in the Riemann tensor there. In curved geometry, a coordinate change cannot make the full curvature tensor vanish at that event.

equationGuide.meaning: Compare two tiny direction-changing steps in opposite orders. In curved geometry the results can differ. The Riemann tensor records this difference. We choose the convention shown in the equation; another book may use the opposite sign, so conventions must stay consistent.

example.title: One curvature contribution
steps: For one contributing component, R = 2 m⁻² and the corresponding dimensionless V component is 3.
That contribution to the derivative difference is 2 × 3 = 6 m⁻².

lessons.title: Add selected curvature components
lessons.idea: Adding selected parts of curvature gives a smaller table of numbers.
body: The Riemann tensor contains the full local curvature information. Contracting loses information; in four dimensions the remaining independent trace-free part is related to the Weyl tensor. This is why Ricci-flat vacuum need not mean flat spacetime.

equationGuide.meaning: A contraction means summing an upper and a lower index with the same label. Doing this to selected Riemann indices gives the Ricci tensor. It keeps part of the curvature information, but not all of it. Empty-space tidal curvature can remain even when Ricci is zero.

example.title: One Ricci component
steps: For one chosen μν pair, the four summed contributions are 1, 2, −1 and 0 m⁻².
Their sum is R_μν = 2 m⁻².

glossary.definition: Summing matching upper and lower index labels.

lessons.title: Relate nearby free-fall paths
lessons.idea: Curvature can make neighbouring free particles accelerate toward or away from each other.
body: This is a one-direction form of geodesic deviation. A uniform coordinate acceleration can be removed locally, but relative tidal acceleration across a region carries curvature information. The separation must remain small enough for the linear approximation.

lessons.title: Include pressure as well as energy
lessons.idea: The stress-energy tensor records energy, momentum and stresses.
body: Energy density and pressure have the same SI dimensions: J/m³ equals Pa. A moving observer generally sees nonzero momentum and energy-flow components. The diagonal form is therefore tied to the fluid rest frame, not to all coordinates.
lessons.equation: T^μν = diag(ε, p, p, p)   (local fluid rest frame)

equationGuide.meaning: Gravity responds to more than a mass count. The stress-energy tensor T describes energy density, momentum flow and stresses. In the local rest frame of a perfect fluid, its diagonal entries are energy density ε and three equal pressures p. Off-diagonal entries vanish in that frame.

example.title: Read a pressure component
steps: A perfect fluid has ε = 10 J/m³ and p = 2 Pa in its local rest frame.
The component T^11 is 2 Pa; it is not the energy-density entry.

lessons.title: Use the local stress-energy balance
lessons.idea: Energy and momentum obey a local balance when every part of the system is included.
body: An individual subsystem can exchange energy and momentum with another, so its divergence need not vanish alone. A global conserved energy requires suitable spacetime structure, such as an appropriate time symmetry and boundary conditions.

equationGuide.meaning: The geometric identity in Einstein’s equation requires a local stress-energy balance. The covariant divergence of the total stress-energy tensor is zero. lessons.title: Recover weak, slow gravity
lessons.idea: General relativity reduces to Newtonian gravity in a suitable limit.
body: The 00 field equation reduces to Poisson’s equation ∇²Φ = 4πG_Nρ for slowly moving matter with negligible pressure compared with rest-energy density. This links the relativistic field equation to its tested weak-field limit.

lessons.title: Find the horizon scale
lessons.idea: A nonrotating black hole has a horizon radius set by its mass.
body: The Schwarzschild metric describes the vacuum exterior of a spherical source. The same radius can be calculated for a star, but a star with surface outside r_s has no horizon at that radius in its actual interior geometry.

equationGuide.meaning: For an isolated, spherical black hole with no spin or electric charge, the horizon is at radius r_s. Double the mass M and this radius doubles. The radius is defined by sphere area: a sphere at r has area 4πr².
