lessons.title: Compare a supported clock with a faraway clock
lessons.idea: A clock held outside a black hole ticks more slowly than a faraway clock.
body: This factor compares specified stationary observers. A falling clock has additional motion and needs its full worldline in the metric. No massive observer can remain static exactly on the horizon.

lessons.title: Measure a gravitational wave’s tiny stretch
lessons.idea: A gravitational wave changes the separation of freely moving test masses.
body: For the perpendicular y arm the sign reverses. A two-arm detector therefore compares two changes, and its response also depends on the wave direction and frequency. A uniform coordinate relabeling cannot remove the wave’s tidal effect.

lessons.title: Separate expansion from motion through space
lessons.idea: The scale factor describes how distances between comoving points change.
body: Cosmic time is proper time for observers moving with the ideal uniform cosmic fluid. Bound systems such as atoms and planetary systems do not simply follow D = aχ with fixed χ, because their internal forces matter.

body: Compare an instrument with a trusted reference. If it reads the same amount too high throughout the range you use, subtract that offset. This corrects the estimated shift. It does not make the reference or the corrected reading perfectly certain.

equationGuide.meaning: Compare an instrument with a trusted reference. If it reads the same amount too high throughout the range you use, subtract that offset. This corrects the estimated shift. It does not make the reference or the corrected reading perfectly certain.

example.title: A scale with a positive offset
steps: A reference check shows that a scale reads 2 g too high. A sample displays 52 g.
The corrected reading is 52 − 2 = 50 g.

lessons.title: Use the mean of repeated readings
lessons.idea: The mean adds repeated readings and divides by how many there are.
body: Repeat the same measurement under the same conditions. The readings may scatter. Their mean gives one estimate of the measured quantity. Averaging can reduce random variation, but a shared offset remains unless it is corrected.
lessons.equation: mean = sum of readings ÷ number of readings

equationGuide.meaning: Repeat the same measurement under the same conditions. The readings may scatter. Their mean gives one estimate of the measured quantity. Averaging can reduce random variation, but a shared offset remains unless it is corrected.

Divide by 3 readings: the mean is 10 mm.

lessons.title: Keep scatter separate from uncertainty of the mean
lessons.idea: Independent repeats can make the mean more precise than one reading.
body: Let s describe the scatter of individual readings, using their sample standard deviation. For n independent readings under stable conditions, divide s by √n to estimate the mean’s standard uncertainty from that scatter. This does not include every source of uncertainty.

equationGuide.meaning: Let s describe the scatter of individual readings, using their sample standard deviation. For n independent readings under stable conditions, divide s by √n to estimate the mean’s standard uncertainty from that scatter. This does not include every source of uncertainty.

example.title: Sixteen independent repeats
steps: The sample standard deviation is s = 8 mm, from n = 16 readings.
The mean’s uncertainty from scatter is 8 ÷ √16 = 2 mm.

lessons.title: Combine independent uncertainty contributions
lessons.idea: Independent standard uncertainties in a sum combine by adding their squares.
body: When adding two measured lengths, square each standard uncertainty, add the squares, then take the square root. This gives the combined standard uncertainty if the errors are independent. It is not a guaranteed maximum error.

The combined standard uncertainty is √(9 + 16) = 5 mm.

lessons.title: Say exactly what you are measuring
lessons.idea: A measurand is the quantity you intend to measure.
body: A clear definition can include the object, time interval, reference frame and averaging rule. Uncertainty in those conditions can contribute to the uncertainty of the result even when the instrument readings look precise.
lessons.equation: average speed = path length / travel time

equationGuide.meaning: “How fast?” is too vague for a measurement. Name the object, the start and finish, and the conditions. If you want average speed over one marked path, measure that path length and the travel time. This definition tells someone else what result to repeat.

example.title: Define one trip
steps: A cart travels a marked 6 m path in 3 s.
Its average speed over that path is 2 m/s.

lessons.terms: Measurand: The particular quantity intended to be measured. Conditions: The circumstances that help define the measurement, such as temperature or path.

glossary.definition: The particular quantity intended to be measured.

lessons.limits: This speed is an average over the stated path. It need not equal the speed at any chosen instant.

lessons.title: Change one cause and compare the result
lessons.idea: A controlled comparison keeps other important conditions the same.
body: Randomizing the order and repeating both conditions helps separate the intended change from drift or uncontrolled differences. A fair comparison still needs an uncertainty estimate and a clear causal design.
lessons.equation: measured effect = changed result − reference result

equationGuide.meaning: To test one change, compare a changed setup with a reference setup. Keep important conditions the same and record them. The difference in results is the measured effect. Hidden changes can also affect that difference, so a difference alone does not prove its cause.

example.title: Compare cooling conditions
steps: Over the same time, a reference cup cools by 4 °C and a cup with a fan cools by 7 °C.
The extra cooling is 7 − 4 = 3 °C.

lessons.terms: Control: The reference condition used for comparison. Confounder: Another changing factor that could explain some of the result.

glossary.definition: The reference condition used for comparison.

lessons.limits: The example assumes comparable cups, starting temperatures and timing. It does not by itself establish a universal cooling law.

lessons.title: Measure the background too
lessons.idea: Subtract a matched background to estimate the signal alone.
body: The background estimate has its own uncertainty. Subtraction removes the estimated average background, not its random fluctuations. A changing background requires a better model or measurements close in time.
lessons.equation: signal rate = total rate − background rate

equationGuide.meaning: An instrument may count both the signal you want and an unrelated background. Measure the background under matching conditions. Subtract it from the total. Use rates if the counting times differ, so you do not subtract counts collected over unequal durations.

example.title: Remove background counts
steps: With a source present, a detector records 120 counts in 10 s. Background alone gives 20 counts in 10 s.
The estimated signal rate is 12 − 2 = 10 counts/s.

glossary.definition: The detector response present without the intended signal.

lessons.limits: Assumes additive, stable background and comparable detector settings. Negative background-subtracted estimates can occur through fluctuations and should not be silently set to zero.

lessons.title: Sample quickly enough for the question
lessons.idea: The spacing between readings limits which changes you can resolve.
body: The ideal sampling theorem assumes a frequency-limited signal. Real filters need a transition region, so practical designs leave a margin below half the sample rate. Sampling quickly does not remove sensor response-time limits.

equationGuide.meaning: If you take evenly spaced readings every Δt seconds, the sample rate is 1/Δt. To recover a signal containing frequencies up to f_max, sample faster than 2f_max and filter out higher frequencies before sampling. Slow sampling can make a fast change appear to be a different slow change.

example.title: Choose a sample rate
steps: Take one reading every 0.1 s, giving 10 readings/s.
This meets the ideal rate condition for a signal limited to frequencies below 5 Hz.

glossary.definition: Number of evenly spaced readings per second.

A device or operation that suppresses selected signal frequencies.

lessons.limits: Evenly spaced sampling and a suitable anti-alias filter. Finite records, noise and sensor bandwidth also limit what can be recovered.

lessons.title: Correct both zero and scale
lessons.idea: A straight-line calibration can correct an offset and a scale error.
body: Two exact points define a straight line, but real calibration uses more points to estimate scatter and inspect departures from a line. The estimated a and b also have uncertainty, often correlated.

equationGuide.meaning: An instrument reading y may follow y = ax + b instead of showing the quantity x directly. The offset b shifts all readings. The gain a changes the scale. Use known reference values to estimate both, then solve for x from a new reading.

example.title: Undo a calibration line
steps: A sensor follows y = 2x + 1, with all values expressed in volts. A new reading is y = 7 V.
The corrected input is (7 − 1)/2 = 3 V.

glossary.definition: Change in instrument output per unit change in input.
Instrument output for zero input.
Establishing the relation between indications and reference values, with uncertainty.

lessons.limits: Use only within a tested range where the straight-line model is suitable. Calibration is not automatically a physical adjustment of the instrument.

lessons.title: Include uncertainty in the reference
lessons.idea: A calibration reference is known with uncertainty, not perfect certainty.
body: Traceability requires a documented chain, not just an instrument label saying “calibrated.” Averaging repeated comparisons may reduce random comparison scatter, but it does not remove a shared reference uncertainty.

equationGuide.meaning: A comparison can be very repeatable while its reference is still uncertain. Include the reference contribution in the calibration result. For two independent standard uncertainties in the same units, square them, add them and take the square root.

example.title: Combine two contributions
steps: A length comparison has standard uncertainty 3 μm and its reference contributes 4 μm independently.
The combined standard uncertainty is √(9 + 16) = 5 μm.

lessons.title: Check the calibration between its endpoints
lessons.idea: Calibration residuals show where a chosen correction misses the reference data.
body: One residual can be ordinary scatter. A pattern across the range, compared with uncertainties, is stronger evidence of an unsuitable model. Use independent check points where possible, and avoid extrapolating beyond the calibrated range.

equationGuide.meaning: For each reference point, compare the observed instrument output with the output predicted by your calibration model. Their difference is a residual. A curved pattern of residuals suggests that a straight-line calibration may be missing a real change in slope.

example.title: Check a middle point
steps: At one reference input, a line predicts 5.0 V but the observed mean output is 5.3 V.
The residual is +0.3 V.

glossary.definition: The measured value minus the model prediction.

lessons.limits: A model diagnostic, not proof from one reading. An uncertain input reference may need an errors-in-variables calibration model.

lessons.title: Check the direction of approach
lessons.idea: Some instruments give different readings depending on their recent history.
body: A single calibration line cannot uniquely undo a history-dependent response unless the history is included. A specified loading procedure, settling time and uncertainty contribution can help manage the effect.
lessons.equation: path difference = reading from above − reading from below

equationGuide.meaning: Approach the same input once from below and once from above. If the readings differ beyond ordinary scatter, the instrument may have hysteresis: its response depends on its recent path. Record the approach direction so others can repeat your procedure.

example.title: Compare two paths
steps: At the same reference force, a gauge reads 10.2 N after decreasing the load and 9.8 N after increasing it.
The path difference is 10.2 − 9.8 = 0.4 N.

glossary.definition: Dependence of a response on its prior path or state.

lessons.limits: Compare the same input and allow the prescribed settling time. Drift, temperature changes and random noise can also cause differences.

lessons.title: Measure how widely readings spread
lessons.idea: Sample standard deviation measures the spread of repeated readings.
body: For independent readings from a stable process, s/√n estimates the random standard uncertainty of the mean. A trend or autocorrelation breaks the simple independent-repeat assumption.

equationGuide.meaning: Subtract the mean from each reading. Square those differences, add them and divide by n − 1. The square root is the sample standard deviation s. It describes the scatter of individual readings; it is not automatically the uncertainty of their mean.

example.title: Find the scatter
steps: Readings 2, 4 and 6 s have mean 4 s and squared deviations 4, 0 and 4 s².
s² = 8/2 = 4 s², so s = 2 s.

glossary.definition: Sample mean.
Number of readings.

lessons.limits: At least two readings. The sample estimates population scatter; small samples give uncertain estimates.

focus.explanation: Subtract the mean from each reading. Square those differences, add them and divide by n − 1. The square root is the sample standard deviation s. It describes the scatter of individual readings; it is not automatically the uncertainty of their mean.

lessons.idea: A shared offset does not disappear when readings are averaged.
body: Random and systematic describe how effects behave. Type A and Type B instead describe how uncertainty is evaluated: from statistical analysis or from other information. A Type B contribution is not automatically a known bias.

equationGuide.meaning: Random scatter changes from reading to reading. A fixed offset shifts them all in the same direction. Averaging can reduce independent scatter, but the shared offset remains. Use a reference to estimate it, then include uncertainty in that correction.

example.title: Average a shared shift
steps: A clock adds the same 0.5 s to every measured interval.
The average of 100 intervals still has that 0.5 s added.

lessons.terms: Bias: A systematic tendency for an estimate to differ from the intended value. b: The shared additive offset in this model.

glossary.definition: A systematic tendency for an estimate to differ from the intended value.
The shared additive offset in this model.

lessons.limits: A constant additive-offset model. Real systematic effects may depend on temperature, range or time.

lessons.title: Allow for rounding on the display
lessons.idea: A rounded display hides values between its steps.
body: This model needs a reason to treat positions within the display step as equally plausible. Identical repeated rounded readings do not prove zero uncertainty. Noise, calibration and drift can add other contributions.

equationGuide.meaning: If a display rounds to the nearest step of width w, the rounding error lies between −w/2 and +w/2. When all values in that range are equally plausible, its standard uncertainty is w/√12. This is one uncertainty contribution, not the whole instrument uncertainty.

example.title: Read a coarse display
steps: A display rounds to the nearest 0.1 V. Its rounding error range is −0.05 to +0.05 V.
The uniform-model standard uncertainty is about 0.029 V.

lessons.terms: Resolution: The smallest indicated change in the stated setting. Uniform model: A model assigning equal probability density within an interval.

glossary.definition: The smallest indicated change in the stated setting.
A model assigning equal probability density within an interval.

lessons.limits: Nearest-step rounding with a uniform error model; truncation or unusual display processing needs a different model.

lessons.title: Track how an input uncertainty affects the result
lessons.idea: A sensitivity factor tells how strongly a result changes with one input.
body: This is the first-order Taylor approximation to uncertainty propagation. Near a turning point the first derivative can be zero even though output uncertainty is not; nonlinear or wide distributions need a higher-order or numerical method.

equationGuide.meaning: For a small input uncertainty, multiply its standard uncertainty by the size of the model’s slope. A steep slope magnifies uncertainty. For y = x², the slope is 2x, so u_y is approximately |2x|u_x.

example.title: Propagate a length uncertainty
steps: For area y = x², let x = 3 m and u_x = 0.1 m.

lessons.terms: Sensitivity factor: The derivative of the result with respect to an input. dy/dx: The local slope of y as x changes.

glossary.definition: The derivative of the result with respect to an input.
The local slope of y as x changes.

lessons.limits: Small uncertainty and a smooth model. Do not use the linear approximation blindly near zero slope or a boundary.

explanations: The first-order approximation can miss curvature.

lessons.title: Include a shared source of uncertainty
lessons.idea: Correlated inputs need a covariance term when uncertainties are combined.
body: For a difference, the covariance term changes sign. A perfectly shared offset can cancel from a difference while remaining in a sum. The signs follow the measurement model’s sensitivity factors.

equationGuide.meaning: If two readings share an uncertain reference, they may move up and down together. For their sum, include twice their covariance as well as their individual variances. Ignoring this shared movement can make the reported uncertainty too small.

example.title: Add correlated readings
steps: Two inputs each have u = 1 V and covariance 1 V².
The sum has variance 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 V², so standard uncertainty 2 V.

lessons.terms: Covariance, cov: A measure of how two uncertain quantities vary together. Variance: The square of a standard deviation or standard uncertainty.

glossary.definition: A measure of how two uncertain quantities vary together.
The square of a standard deviation or standard uncertainty.

lessons.limits: The formula is exact for the variance of a sum. Covariance values must be compatible with the individual variances; |cov| cannot exceed u_xu_y.

explanations: Yes. Subtracting identical shared shifts cancels them.
The signs in the model matter.

lessons.title: Fit a line by its squared misses
lessons.idea: Least squares chooses parameters that minimize squared residuals.
body: For a line y = a + bx with equally uncertain independent y readings and negligible x uncertainty, b = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)² and a = ȳ−bx̄. Minimizing the score does not prove the model describes the physics.

equationGuide.meaning: A model prediction rarely passes through every noisy reading. Least squares adds the squares of the vertical misses and chooses the model parameters that make this sum smallest. Squaring prevents positive and negative misses from canceling.

example.title: Score one candidate line
steps: A candidate line has residuals −1, 0 and 2 V.
Its score is 1 + 0 + 4 = 5 V².

lessons.terms: ŷ_i: Model prediction for reading i. Parameter: A number adjusted to fit the model, such as slope. Least squares: Fitting by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.

glossary.definition: Model prediction for reading i.
A number adjusted to fit the model, such as slope.
Fitting by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.

lessons.limits: Ordinary least squares treats input x as effectively known. Unequal or correlated uncertainties need an appropriate fitting method.

lessons.title: Give precise readings more weight
lessons.idea: Inverse-variance weighting gives less influence to noisier readings.
body: A weighted mean of a common constant is Σw_i y_i/Σw_i. Correlated readings require a covariance matrix rather than just independent weights; very optimistic uncertainty estimates can give one faulty reading too much influence.

equationGuide.meaning: If readings have different known standard uncertainties, do not treat them as equally precise. Give reading i weight 1/u_i². A reading with twice the uncertainty gets one quarter of the weight, not half.

example.title: Compare weights
steps: One reading has u = 1 V and another has u = 2 V.
Their weights are 1 and 0.25 V⁻²: the first has four times the weight.

lessons.terms: Weight, w: The factor multiplying a squared residual in the fit. u_i: Standard uncertainty assigned to reading i.

glossary.definition: The factor multiplying a squared residual in the fit.
Standard uncertainty assigned to reading i.

lessons.limits: Independent readings, suitable model and reliable uncertainty estimates. This is not permission to choose weights just to obtain a preferred answer.

explanations: More uncertainty means less weight here.

lessons.title: Compare misses with expected uncertainty
lessons.idea: Reduced chi-square compares squared scaled residuals with remaining freedom.
body: Interpretation relies on the noise model. A large value may indicate underestimated uncertainties, correlations, outliers or a poor model. A very small value may reflect overestimated uncertainty or excessive fitting flexibility.

equationGuide.meaning: Divide each residual by its known standard uncertainty, then add the squares to get χ². Divide by n − p, where n is the number of independent readings and p is the number of fitted parameters. A value near one can be reasonable; it is not proof that the model is true.

example.title: Count remaining freedom
steps: A suitable fit has χ² = 6 from 8 independent readings and 2 fitted parameters.

lessons.terms: χ²: Chi-square: sum of squared uncertainty-scaled residuals. n − p: Residual degrees of freedom in this regular fit. p: Number of independently fitted parameters.

glossary.definition: Chi-square: sum of squared uncertainty-scaled residuals.
Residual degrees of freedom in this regular fit.
Number of independently fitted parameters.

lessons.limits: Standard chi-square interpretation assumes independent Gaussian errors, known variances and a suitable regular model. Nonlinear or constrained fits can need more care.

lessons.title: Check predictions on data the fit did not use
lessons.idea: A model should predict new readings as well as fit old ones.
body: If you repeatedly tune against the same held-out data, it becomes part of model selection and loses its role as a fresh check. Residual plots, physics and genuinely new data provide complementary evidence.

equationGuide.meaning: Save some suitable data for checking after fitting. Compare the model’s predictions with these held-out readings. A flexible curve can follow old noise very closely and still predict poorly. Keep the check independent of repeated tuning.

example.title: Try a new reading
steps: A fitted model predicts 4.0 V for an independent check point. The check reads 5.0 V.
The prediction error is 1.0 V; compare it with the full prediction uncertainty.

lessons.terms: Held-out data: Data excluded from fitting and tuning. Overfitting: Following sample-specific noise so closely that new predictions suffer.

glossary.definition: Data excluded from fitting and tuning.

lessons.limits: Check points must represent the intended use. Uncertainty of model parameters and of new readings both matter.

lessons.title: Keep the raw readings and the rule
lessons.idea: A repeatable record shows how raw readings became a result.
body: A useful procedure also states the measurand, equipment, sampling order, settling time, exclusions and uncertainty method. Versioned analysis code helps reproduce calculations, while new experiments test reproducibility under changed conditions.
lessons.equation: corrected result = recorded reading − recorded offset

equationGuide.meaning: Save the original readings, units, settings and times. Record the calculation and calibration version separately. Someone else should be able to start from the saved readings and obtain your result. Keep corrections visible instead of replacing the only copy of the raw data.

example.title: Rebuild one result
steps: A record says: reading 12.4 V; offset 0.3 V; calibration version A; stable room temperature.
The recorded rule gives 12.1 V, and the raw 12.4 V remains available.

lessons.title: Repeat a reference during the run
lessons.idea: A reference checked over time can reveal instrument drift.
body: Interleaving reference checks and changing the order of test conditions can expose drift that would otherwise look like an experimental effect. A straight-line drift correction needs evidence that the drift actually followed that pattern.
lessons.equation: observed drift = end reference reading − start reference reading

equationGuide.meaning: Measure the same stable reference near the start and end of a run. A changed reading may reveal drift: the instrument response changes with time. Compare the change with its uncertainty before deciding it is significant.

example.title: Check one run
steps: A stable reference reads 5.00 V at the start and 5.06 V at the end.
The observed shift is +0.06 V; its significance depends on the check uncertainty.

lessons.terms: Drift: A gradual change in an instrument’s response over time. Check standard: A reference measured to monitor the measurement process.

glossary.definition: A gradual change in an instrument’s response over time.
A reference measured to monitor the measurement process.

lessons.limits: A two-point check cannot reveal every change between the endpoints. The reference itself must be sufficiently stable.

lessons.title: State the width and how it was chosen
lessons.idea: Expanded uncertainty multiplies standard uncertainty by a stated coverage factor.
body: A normal distribution with effectively known standard deviation has about 95% within roughly two standard deviations. Small samples or other distributions require different coverage calculations. The interval is a model-based uncertainty statement, not a guarantee.

equationGuide.meaning: A report may give a result as y ± U. Here U = ku_c, where u_c is combined standard uncertainty and k is the coverage factor. State k and the assumptions used. Calling every k = 2 interval “exactly 95%” is not justified.

example.title: Expand an uncertainty
steps: A measurement has u_c = 0.3 V. Choose k = 2 under a suitable near-normal, well-supported model.
Report U = 0.6 V, with k = 2 and the model stated.

lessons.terms: Expanded uncertainty, U: A stated multiple of combined standard uncertainty. Coverage factor, k: The multiplier chosen for the intended coverage under the model.

glossary.definition: A stated multiple of combined standard uncertainty.

lessons.limits: State the distribution assumptions and effective degrees of freedom when relevant. Confidence and Bayesian credible intervals have distinct interpretations.

lessons.title: Match reported digits to the uncertainty
lessons.idea: Extra calculated digits do not create extra knowledge.
body: The choice of one or two significant digits in uncertainty follows the reporting convention and context. Also report the tested range, model assumptions and important unmeasured effects; a small uncertainty applies only to the defined measurand and model.
lessons.equation: rounded result and uncertainty → same decimal place

equationGuide.meaning: Keep guard digits while calculating, then round the final uncertainty sensibly and the result to the same decimal place. Give the unit, conditions and uncertainty meaning. This lets a reader see the useful precision without mistaking calculator digits for measured detail.

lessons.title: Read the two amplitudes of a qubit
lessons.idea: A pure qubit state uses two amplitudes to predict two measurement outcomes.
body: Write the state as a|0⟩ + b|1⟩. The labels 0 and 1 name the outcomes of the chosen measurement. The amplitudes a and b are numbers that may be complex. Square the magnitude of an amplitude to find its outcome’s probability. Both probabilities must add to one.

equationGuide.meaning: Write the state as a|0⟩ + b|1⟩. The labels 0 and 1 name the outcomes of the chosen measurement. The amplitudes a and b are numbers that may be complex. Square the magnitude of an amplitude to find its outcome’s probability. Both probabilities must add to one.

example.title: A normalized qubit
steps: Take real amplitudes a = 0.6 and b = 0.8.
The probabilities are 0.36 and 0.64. They add to 1.

lessons.terms: Qubit: A quantum system with two basis states. Pure state: One quantum state described by amplitudes, rather than a statistical mixture of different states. Amplitude: A number used to calculate measurement probabilities and interference. |0⟩ and |1⟩: Labels for two distinct basis states, read as ket zero and ket one. |a|: Magnitude, or size, of amplitude a.

glossary.definition: A quantum system with two basis states.
One quantum state described by amplitudes, rather than a statistical mixture of different states.
A number used to calculate measurement probabilities and interference.
Labels for two distinct basis states, read as ket zero and ket one.

lessons.limits: This describes a pure state and a measurement in the stated 0/1 basis. Mixed states need a density matrix. Amplitudes are not probabilities themselves.

lessons.title: Change a relative sign with a Z gate
lessons.idea: A relative sign can change a state even when its 0/1 probabilities stay the same.
body: The Z gate leaves the |0⟩ amplitude alone and reverses the sign of the |1⟩ amplitude. Squaring magnitudes hides that sign in a direct 0/1 measurement. A later gate can make the sign difference affect what we observe.

lessons.title: Turn a relative sign into a definite outcome
lessons.idea: A Hadamard gate can turn a relative sign difference into different measurement outcomes.
body: The Hadamard gate, called H, combines amplitudes by adding and subtracting them. Matching signs reinforce one output; opposite signs reinforce the other. This is interference. It lets a later measurement distinguish the plus and minus states.

lessons.title: Choose which question to ask the qubit
lessons.idea: A measurement probability depends on the chosen basis.
body: An X-basis measurement uses |+⟩ and |−⟩. It can be implemented by applying H and then measuring in the 0/1 basis. Probabilities sum to one for a complete orthonormal basis.

equationGuide.meaning: A qubit can be measured along different bases. To find the chance of a basis outcome |v⟩, take its overlap with the state |ψ⟩ and square the magnitude. A state that is certain in one basis can be uncertain in another.

steps: The state is |0⟩ and |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. The overlap is 1/√2.

lessons.title: Update the state after a known outcome
lessons.idea: An ideal projective measurement prepares the state associated with its result.
body: For a general projector P, the conditional state is P|ψ⟩/√⟨ψ|P|ψ⟩ when that outcome has nonzero probability. If the outcome is discarded, use a mixture of possible post-measurement states.

equationGuide.meaning: Suppose a 0/1 measurement returns 0. Conditioned on that result, the qubit is now |0⟩. Immediately repeating the same ideal measurement gives 0 again. This rule uses the result you actually observed; it does not say you could choose that first result.

lessons.title: Keep probabilities for different preparations
lessons.idea: A density matrix describes a mixture as well as a pure state.
body: For |+⟩, ρ has off-diagonal entries 1/2. A half-zero, half-one mixture has zero off-diagonal entries. Measuring in the X basis distinguishes these preparations statistically, although a 0/1 measurement does not.

equationGuide.meaning: If a preparation chooses |0⟩ with chance p and |1⟩ with chance 1 − p, write those chances on the diagonal of a density matrix ρ. This mixture records uncertain preparation. It is different from one coherent superposition, even when 0/1 probabilities match.

example.title: Read a mixture
steps: A preparation chooses |0⟩ with chance 0.7 and |1⟩ with chance 0.3.
Its density matrix has diagonal entries 0.7 and 0.3; P(1) = 0.3.

lessons.title: Tell a pure state from a mixture
lessons.idea: Purity is one for a pure state and smaller for a mixed state.
body: A qubit’s purity lies between 1/2 and 1. The complete two-qubit state can be pure while either qubit alone is mixed; correlations with another system are another reason a local density matrix can be mixed.
lessons.equation: purity = Tr(ρ²);   diagonal qubit: p² + (1 − p)²

equationGuide.meaning: Multiply the density matrix by itself and add its diagonal entries. This number, Tr(ρ²), is purity. For a diagonal qubit mixture with probabilities p and 1 − p, it is p² + (1 − p)². A mixed qubit can have uncertain outcomes without being a pure superposition.

example.title: Check a balanced mixture
steps: Use p = 1/2 for a half-zero, half-one mixture.
Purity is 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

lessons.title: Combine two independent qubits
lessons.idea: A product state multiplies the amplitudes of its two parts.
body: Not every two-qubit state is a product. Entangled pure states cannot be written as one tensor product of separate qubit states; their joint probabilities need not factor.

equationGuide.meaning: Write the first qubit on the left and the second on the right. For separately prepared qubits, multiply their amplitudes to get each joint amplitude. The label |01⟩ means first qubit 0, second qubit 1. Keep this order fixed throughout a calculation.

steps: The first qubit has P(1) = 0.4 and the independent second has P(0) = 0.5.

lessons.idea: Changing the order of two gates can change the final state.
body: For the reversed order HZ on |0⟩, Z first leaves |0⟩ unchanged and H then gives |+⟩. A 0/1 measurement hides the difference, but an X-basis measurement reveals it.

lessons.title: Undo gates in reverse order
lessons.idea: The inverse circuit reverses the order and undoes each gate.
body: For a longer product U_3U_2U_1, the inverse is U_1†U_2†U_3†. Noise can leak information into an environment, so reversing the intended gates alone does not generally reverse the physical process.

equationGuide.meaning: An ideal unitary gate has an inverse. To undo several gates, undo the last one first. H and X each undo themselves. If you applied H then X, undo with X then H. Measurement that discards a result is not generally reversible this way.

example.title: Undo a two-gate circuit
steps: Start in |0⟩, apply H then X, and then apply X then H.

lessons.idea: CNOT uses one qubit to control an X operation on another.
body: Applying CNOT twice restores every input state, including superpositions. It can entangle two qubits, but it does not make independent copies of an arbitrary unknown quantum state.

lessons.title: Prepare two qubits with linked outcomes
lessons.idea: A Bell pair is a joint state that cannot be split into two separate pure states.
body: For a pure joint state, failure to factor into a product establishes entanglement. Matching results in only one basis do not establish it: a classical mixture of 00 and 11 would also match in that basis.

equationGuide.meaning: Start with |00⟩. Apply H to the first qubit, then CNOT with that qubit as control. The result has equal amplitudes for |00⟩ and |11⟩. A 0/1 measurement gives matching results, but neither individual result is fixed in advance by this state description.

example.title: Read a Bell pair
steps: Prepare |Φ⁺⟩ and measure both qubits in the 0/1 basis.
Outcomes 00 and 11 each have probability 1/2; 01 and 10 have probability zero.

lessons.terms: Entangled state: A joint state that cannot be described as a mixture of separate product states. Bell pair: One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states.

glossary.definition: A joint state that cannot be described as a mixture of separate product states.
One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states.

lessons.limits: Ideal two-qubit preparation, fixed ket order and ideal measurements. A noisy preparation needs evidence beyond the intended circuit.

explanations: Other measurement settings distinguish the preparations.

lessons.title: Compare the same pair in a second basis
lessons.idea: A coherent Bell pair and a classical mixture can agree in one basis but differ in another.
body: For |Φ⁺⟩, expressing both qubits in the X basis gives (|++⟩ + |−−⟩)/√2. A mixture lacks the cross terms responsible for this interference. Entanglement tests need stated assumptions and reliable measurement settings.
lessons.equation: P(same X outcomes): Bell Φ⁺ = 1; half-00/half-11 mixture = 1/2

equationGuide.meaning: The Bell state |Φ⁺⟩ also gives matching results when both qubits are measured in the plus/minus basis. A half-00, half-11 mixture does not: in that basis its four outcome pairs are equally likely. The second basis reveals information that 0/1 results missed.

example.title: Test the mixture in X
steps: Use the half-00, half-11 mixture and measure both qubits in the X basis.
The four pairs ++, +−, −+ and −− each have probability 1/4; matching pairs total 1/2.

lessons.terms: X basis: The plus/minus basis. Coherence: Relative-phase information that can affect interference.

glossary.definition: The plus/minus basis.
Relative-phase information that can affect interference.

lessons.limits: These are ideal predictions for the two specified preparations. They do not claim that any single pair of matching readings certifies entanglement.

lessons.title: Look at what one observer can see
lessons.idea: An observer sees local probabilities unless the other result is communicated.
body: Conditioning on a known remote result changes the appropriate state description. Learning that result still requires a communication channel. Quantum teleportation also needs classical messages for this reason.

equationGuide.meaning: For a Bell pair, either observer alone sees 0 or 1 with equal chances. A distant choice of measurement, with its outcome unreported, does not change those local statistics. Correlations become visible when the observers compare records through ordinary communication.

example.title: Ignore the second record
steps: The first observer sees 0 with probability 1/2.

lessons.terms: Marginal probability: A local probability found by summing over the other outcomes. No-signalling: Local outcome statistics cannot be controlled by a remote measurement choice alone.

glossary.definition: A local probability found by summing over the other outcomes.
Local outcome statistics cannot be controlled by a remote measurement choice alone.

lessons.limits: Standard quantum mechanics and local trace-preserving operations when remote results are not selected and announced.

lessons.title: Compare correlations with a local-model bound
lessons.idea: A Bell test compares measured correlations across several measurement choices.
body: Quantum theory permits |S| up to 2√2. Real claims require uncertainty analysis and careful treatment of detection, locality and setting-choice loopholes. A violation excludes the tested class of models; it does not enable faster-than-light signalling.

equationGuide.meaning: In a CHSH test, each observer chooses one of two settings and records +1 or −1. E is the average product of their results for a setting pair. Suitable local hidden-variable models satisfy |S| ≤ 2. Quantum predictions can exceed this bound with appropriate entangled states and settings.

example.title: Combine correlations
steps: Suppose the four estimated correlations are 0.6, 0.6, 0.6 and −0.6 in the displayed order.
S = 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.6 − (−0.6) = 2.4, above the local bound.

lessons.terms: CHSH: A Bell-inequality test using two binary settings per observer. Local hidden-variable model: A model with local outcome rules and shared prior variables, under the test’s independence assumptions.

glossary.definition: A Bell-inequality test using two binary settings per observer.
A model with local outcome rules and shared prior variables, under the test’s independence assumptions.

lessons.limits: The bound relies on the stated local-model and independent-setting assumptions. Toy correlations omit sampling uncertainty and experimental loopholes.

focus.idea: A Bell test compares measured correlations across several measurement choices.
focus.explanation: In a CHSH test, each observer chooses one of two settings and records +1 or −1. E is the average product of their results for a setting pair. example.title: Combine correlations

terms.definition: A Bell-inequality test using two binary settings per observer.

check.prompt: Does a CHSH violation allow controllable faster-than-light signalling?
explanations: A correlation bound is not a communication channel.

Yes. Quantum correlations still obey no-signalling.

lessons.title: Mix a state with its flipped version
lessons.idea: A bit-flip channel applies X with probability p.
body: For input probability q = P(0), the output is P(0) = (1−p)q + p(1−q). Other entries also transform; a population calculation alone does not describe every property of the qubit.

equationGuide.meaning: A noisy qubit may be flipped or left alone. If the flip chance is p, its output density matrix is the weighted sum of those two possibilities. This describes an average over unknown errors, not a coherent superposition of “flip” and “no flip.”

example.title: Track an input zero
steps: Send |0⟩ through a channel with flip chance 0.1.
The output gives 0 with chance 0.9 and 1 with chance 0.1.

lessons.terms: Channel: A physical rule mapping an input density matrix to an output density matrix. p: Probability of a flip, between zero and one.

glossary.definition: A physical rule mapping an input density matrix to an output density matrix.
Probability of a flip, between zero and one.

lessons.limits: Single-qubit stochastic X errors with a specified probability. Real devices can have correlated, coherent or state-dependent errors.

lessons.title: Lose phase information without changing populations
lessons.idea: Random phase flips can weaken the link between two amplitudes.
body: At p = 1, the channel is a known Z gate and remains reversible; it does not erase phase information. Maximum loss for this random-flip family occurs at p = 1/2, so “more p means more decoherence” is not true over the whole interval.

equationGuide.meaning: A Z error reverses the sign of the |1⟩ amplitude. If it occurs with probability p, a density matrix’s off-diagonal entry c becomes (1 − 2p)c. Its 0/1 probabilities stay the same. At p = 1/2, those off-diagonal entries vanish.

example.title: Erase one coherence
steps: A |+⟩ state has off-diagonal entry 0.5. Apply a random Z with chance 0.5.
The new entry is zero, leaving a half-zero, half-one mixture.

lessons.terms: Off-diagonal coherence, c: A density-matrix entry carrying relative-phase information in the chosen basis. Phase-flip channel: The map (1−p)ρ + pZρZ.

glossary.definition: A density-matrix entry carrying relative-phase information in the chosen basis.
The map (1−p)ρ + pZρZ.

lessons.limits: Z-basis phase-flip model with 0 ≤ p ≤ 1. This lesson does not equate all dephasing conventions with the same p.

focus.idea: Random phase flips can weaken the link between two amplitudes.
focus.explanation: A Z error reverses the sign of the |1⟩ amplitude. In a density matrix, entries away from the main diagonal record this phase-sensitive link. Call one such entry c. If the error chance is p, it becomes (1 − 2p)c. The 0/1 probabilities stay the same. At p = 1/2, c becomes zero.

example.title: Erase one coherence
steps: A |+⟩ state has off-diagonal entry 0.5. Apply a random Z with chance 0.5.
The new entry is zero, leaving a half-zero, half-one mixture.

terms.definition: A density-matrix entry carrying relative-phase information in the chosen basis.
The map (1−p)ρ + pZρZ.

options: No, it is a definite Z gate
explanations: The operation is unitary for every input at p = 1.
Yes. A known Z operation can be undone.

lessons.title: Model loss from the excited state
lessons.idea: An excited qubit can lose energy and end up in its lower state.
body: In this channel the off-diagonal entry is also multiplied by √(1−γ). A pure superposition may therefore become mixed. A finite-temperature environment can also excite the qubit and needs a more general model.

equationGuide.meaning: Label |1⟩ as excited and |0⟩ as ground. In a simple zero-temperature relaxation model, a fraction γ of the excited population decays. The remaining excited probability is (1 − γ) times its starting value. The lost population appears in |0⟩.

example.title: Lose excited population
steps: Start with P(1) = 0.8 and decay probability γ = 0.25.

lessons.terms: γ: Decay probability over the modeled interval. Relaxation: Transfer toward a lower-energy state through coupling to the environment.

glossary.definition: Decay probability over the modeled interval.
Transfer toward a lower-energy state through coupling to the environment.

lessons.limits: Zero-temperature single-qubit amplitude damping; 0 ≤ γ ≤ 1. The equation displayed tracks one population, not the complete state.

focus.idea: An excited qubit can lose energy and end up in its lower state.
focus.explanation: Label the excited state |1⟩ and the lower state |0⟩. In this simple cooling model, a fraction γ of the excited population decays. The remaining chance of finding |1⟩ is (1 − γ) times its starting value. The lost probability moves to |0⟩.

example.title: Lose excited population
steps: Start with P(1) = 0.8 and decay probability γ = 0.25.

terms.definition: Decay probability over the modeled interval.

check.prompt: Is the lost excited population removed from total probability?
explanations: Relaxation changes populations, not normalization.

lessons.title: Check that a channel preserves probability
lessons.idea: A noise model must keep the total probability equal to one.
body: Different Kraus sets can represent the same channel. Their individual terms are not unique physical stories unless a particular environmental measurement is specified. Complete positivity ensures compatibility with untouched ancillary systems.
lessons.equation: ρ_out = Σ K_jρK_j†;   Σ K_j†K_j = I

equationGuide.meaning: A general channel can add terms K_jρK_j†. The dagger means conjugate transpose. To keep total probability one for every input, the operators must satisfy ΣK_j†K_j = I. This form also keeps states valid when they are part of an entangled system.

example.title: Check a bit-flip model
steps: Use K_0 = √0.8 I and K_1 = √0.2 X. Since X†X = I, their products are 0.8I and 0.2I.
The sum is I, so this channel preserves total probability.

lessons.terms: Kraus operators, K_j: Operators specifying one representation of a quantum channel. I: Identity operator. †: Conjugate transpose: transpose and complex conjugate.

glossary.definition: Operators specifying one representation of a quantum channel.
Identity operator.
Conjugate transpose: transpose and complex conjugate.

lessons.limits: Finite-dimensional channel with all outcomes retained. A selected measurement branch alone need not preserve trace until conditioned and normalized.

focus.idea: A noise model must keep the total probability equal to one.
focus.explanation: The matrices K_j describe possible effects of the noise. Add their contributions to get the output state. The dagger means swap rows and columns, then reverse imaginary parts. The rule ΣK_j†K_j = I keeps total probability equal to one, even when the qubit is part of a larger entangled system.
focus.equation: ρ_out = Σ K_jρK_j†;   Σ K_j†K_j = I

example.title: Check a bit-flip model
steps: Use K_0 = √0.8 I and K_1 = √0.2 X. Since X†X = I, their products are 0.8I and 0.2I.
The sum is I, so this channel preserves total probability.

terms.definition: Operators specifying one representation of a quantum channel.
Identity operator.
Conjugate transpose: transpose and complex conjugate.

options: Only if two operators are used
explanations: Yes. Different sets can describe the same channel.

lessons.title: Spread one logical qubit across three physical qubits
lessons.idea: Encoding stores one qubit jointly rather than making independent copies.
body: Two CNOTs from the original qubit to blank targets implement this encoding. Linearity produces a joint superposition of 000 and 111, not the tensor cube of the input state. A phase error can still damage its logical information.

equationGuide.meaning: The three-qubit bit-flip code maps a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ to a|000⟩ + b|111⟩. The amplitudes are stored in the whole group. This is not three independent copies of the original unknown state. The code is designed to correct one physical bit flip.

example.title: Encode one state
steps: Start with 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩ and two blank qubits in |00⟩.
Controlled flips produce 0.6|000⟩ + 0.8|111⟩; P(111) = 0.64.

lessons.terms: Logical qubit: Information stored in a chosen encoded subspace. Physical qubit: One actual two-level system used in the encoding. No-cloning: No fixed physical operation can perfectly copy every unknown quantum state into independent copies.

glossary.definition: Information stored in a chosen encoded subspace.
One actual two-level system used in the encoding.
No fixed physical operation can perfectly copy every unknown quantum state into independent copies.

lessons.limits: Ideal three-qubit repetition code protecting against a single X error. It does not correct general single-qubit errors.

lessons.title: Read an error pattern without reading the logical bit
lessons.idea: Parity checks can locate a bit flip without revealing the encoded amplitudes.
body: Ancilla qubits can collect the two parities through controlled gates. Measuring all three data qubits individually would instead reveal the logical 0/1 branch and destroy an arbitrary logical superposition.

equationGuide.meaning: Check whether qubits 1 and 2 agree, and whether 2 and 3 agree. Record 0 for agreement and 1 for disagreement. For a single middle-qubit flip, both checks are 1. Measuring these parities preserves the unknown logical superposition while identifying the correctable error.

example.title: Locate a middle error
steps: A middle flip changes a|000⟩ + b|111⟩ into a|010⟩ + b|101⟩.
Both components give syndrome (1,1); flipping the middle qubit restores the code state.

lessons.terms: Syndrome: The outcomes of error checks, used to choose a correction. Parity check: A measurement of agreement or disagreement rather than each individual value.

glossary.definition: The outcomes of error checks, used to choose a correction.
A measurement of agreement or disagreement rather than each individual value.

lessons.limits: Ideal encoding, parity measurement and correction, with at most one X error. Multiple errors can produce a misleading syndrome.

lessons.title: Count the errors a small code misses
lessons.idea: The three-bit majority code fails when at least two independent bits flip.
body: This expression is smaller than p for 0 < p < 1/2 under the ideal assumptions. Fault-tolerant designs also account for faults introduced by gates, checks and recovery; merely adding qubits does not guarantee better information.

equationGuide.meaning: With independent flip chance p on each of three qubits and perfect correction, zero or one flip is corrected. Two or three flips cause a logical error. Add those probabilities to estimate the failure chance. The benefit depends on the physical error rate and the correction process.

example.title: Estimate failure
steps: Use independent p = 0.1 and ideal correction.

lessons.title: Put a function value into an amplitude sign
lessons.idea: A phase oracle changes signs according to a function.
body: A reversible bit oracle |x,y⟩ → |x,y⊕f(x)⟩ gives this phase action when its target is |−⟩. This is phase kickback. An oracle call is an assumed resource; constructing the oracle can itself cost substantial work.

equationGuide.meaning: For a bit-valued function f(x), a phase oracle multiplies |x⟩ by (−1)^f(x). Inputs with f(x) = 1 get a minus sign. A direct measurement in the x basis cannot see that sign. A later interference step can turn it into different outcome probabilities.

example.title: Mark one basis term
steps: For f(0) = 0 and f(1) = 1, start with |+⟩.
The oracle gives (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 = |−⟩.

lessons.terms: Oracle: A specified operation providing access to a function. Phase oracle: An oracle storing the function value in a relative amplitude phase.

glossary.definition: A specified operation providing access to a function.
An oracle storing the function value in a relative amplitude phase.

lessons.limits: Ideal promised oracle. A sign common to the whole state is a global phase and cannot be observed by itself.

body: The constant subtraction in the mean-field Hamiltonian prevents double-counting bond energies. It does not change a single spin’s probability ratio, but it matters for free energy and comparison of candidate states.

body: Below the mean-field transition, the zero solution remains algebraically present but is unstable in the free-energy picture. Nonzero solutions can appear, and a free-energy comparison selects stable equilibrium candidates.

equationGuide.meaning: A spin in field energy h_eff has average tanh(h_eff/(k_BT)). But h_eff itself depends on the average m. Choose m so that the predicted average equals the assumed one. A trial update is a way to seek a solution; it is not a physical time step.

steps: Set h = 0 and try m = 0 at a nonzero temperature.

lessons.title: Relate equilibrium fluctuations to a static response
lessons.idea: In a classical equilibrium model, stronger fluctuations can mean a stronger response.
body: This follows by differentiating thermal probabilities with respect to h. In quantum systems where M does not commute with the Hamiltonian, the static relation generally requires an imaginary-time correlation rather than just equal-time variance.

equationGuide.meaning: Let an applied field enter the energy as −hM, where M is a dimensionless total spin. At fixed temperature, the response χ = ∂⟨M⟩/∂h equals Var(M)/(k_BT). The same fluctuations present before the field changes help determine the response to a small change.

example.title: Use equilibrium variance
steps: A classical equilibrium system has Var(M) = 4 and k_BT = 2 energy units.
Its static susceptibility is 2 per energy unit.

lessons.title: Give each place its own field value
lessons.idea: A classical field assigns a value to each place and time.
body: A scalar field assigns one number to each place. Call it φ(x, t): the value at position x and time t. A moving particle has one changing position; a field describes values across space. Quantum field theory begins with fields, then changes how we describe their states.

lessons.title: Give a free boson mode discrete energy levels
lessons.idea: A free boson mode has the energy levels of a quantum harmonic oscillator.
body: Its occupation number n can be 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each extra quantum raises the energy by the same gap ε. Including the oscillator’s ground energy, the level is (n + 1/2)ε. Here ε is Planck’s reduced constant times the mode’s angular frequency.

equationGuide.meaning: Its occupation number n can be 0, 1, 2 and so on. Each extra quantum raises the energy by the same gap ε. Including the oscillator’s ground energy, the level is (n + 1/2)ε. Here ε is Planck’s reduced constant times the mode’s angular frequency.

example.title: One mode with two quanta
steps: Take a mode with energy gap ε = 4 energy units and occupation n = 2.
Its oscillator energy is (2 + 1/2) × 4 = 10 energy units.

lessons.title: Choose units that simplify the writing
lessons.idea: Natural units set the numerical values of c and ℏ to one.
body: Time and length then have inverse-energy units. Returning to SI restores E² = p²c² + m²c⁴. The following modules use natural units unless a lesson explicitly says otherwise.

equationGuide.meaning: The laws have the same meaning, but the chosen units make the speed of light c and reduced Planck constant ℏ equal to one. Then mass, momentum and energy can use the same energy unit. This is a choice of measuring scales, not a claim that the constants vanish.

steps: Use natural units and a particle mass m = 3 GeV with momentum p = 0.

lessons.title: Add the local contributions across space and time
lessons.idea: Action adds a field’s contributions across space and time.
body: Action is not generally ordinary energy and stationary does not always mean smallest. Boundary conditions specify which field variations are allowed when deriving the motion equation.

equationGuide.meaning: A field changes at many places at once. Its Lagrangian density ℒ gives a local contribution. Add that contribution over space and time to obtain the action S. A stationary action means a tiny allowed change of the field history has no first-order effect on S.

example.title: Add a constant contribution
steps: In natural units, ℒ = 2 GeV⁴ throughout a region of spacetime volume 3 GeV⁻⁴.
That region contributes S = 6, a dimensionless action in these units.

lessons.terms: ℒ: Lagrangian density: the contribution to action per space and time volume. ∫: An integral: addition over a continuous range. d³x dt: A tiny space volume multiplied by a tiny time interval.

glossary.definition: Lagrangian density: the contribution to action per space and time volume.
An integral: addition over a continuous range.
A tiny space volume multiplied by a tiny time interval.

lessons.limits: Classical real scalar field in flat spacetime; ℏ = c = 1. The constant-region calculation is a bookkeeping example, not necessarily a solution of the field equation.

focus.idea: Action adds a field’s contributions across space and time.

lessons.title: Separate changing, sloping and restoring parts
lessons.idea: A free scalar field has a simple Lagrangian density built from three parts.
body: The associated energy density has positive signs for all three terms when m² ≥ 0. The different signs in ℒ encode the motion law; they do not mean the spatial-gradient energy is negative.

equationGuide.meaning: The field φ can change with time and slope across space. The free-field density contains a positive time-change term, a negative spatial-slope term and a negative restoring term set by mass m. “Free” means there is no extra interaction term.

lessons.title: Use a local rule for how the field changes
lessons.idea: The free scalar field obeys the Klein–Gordon equation.
body: For a density depending on φ and its first derivatives, the field Euler–Lagrange rule is ∂_μ[∂ℒ/∂(∂_μφ)] − ∂ℒ/∂φ = 0. Applying it to the preceding density gives the displayed equation.

equationGuide.meaning: The field’s time change is linked to its spatial bending and its mass term. The action rule gives the Klein–Gordon equation. In a spatially uniform field, there is no spatial bending, so each field value follows an oscillator-like restoring rule.

example.title: Use a uniform field
steps: In natural units, a uniform field has m = 2 GeV and φ = 3 GeV at an instant.
With ∇²φ = 0, its time curvature is ∂t²φ = −4×3 = −12 GeV³.

lessons.title: Replace mode variables by operators
lessons.idea: For a quantum mode, the order of two operations matters.
body: With orthonormal real spatial modes, these rules give the equal-time field relation [φ(x),π(y)] = iδ³(x−y). The spatial delta is a distribution, so fields at exact points require care; averaging over regions gives meaningful smeared operators.

equationGuide.meaning: Choose independent real field modes. Each mode has an amplitude Q and a paired momentum P. Quantization makes them operators with [Q,P] = i in natural units. The order QP therefore differs from PQ. This is the same rule used for a quantum oscillator.

lessons.title: Build the field from quantum mode amplitudes
lessons.idea: A quantum field combines spatial patterns with operator amplitudes.

lessons.title: Connect two interaction points in a diagram
lessons.idea: An internal propagator is a calculation factor, not a directly observed particle path.
body: Vertices conserve four-momentum in a translation-invariant theory. Internal lines are parts of a perturbation expansion, not separately measured particles borrowing energy for a short time. The iε prescription defines how singular poles are handled.

equationGuide.meaning: A scalar internal line carries a momentum p and contributes i/(p² − m² + iε). It joins interaction points in the amplitude calculation. Its momentum need not satisfy p² = m². That does not let the full process ignore energy and momentum conservation.

example.title: Inspect an off-shell denominator
steps: Use invariant p² = 10 GeV² and m² = 4 GeV², away from the pole.
The real part of the denominator is 6 GeV²; this internal momentum is off shell.

lessons.title: Add indistinguishable contributions before squaring
lessons.idea: Contributions to the same outcome can reinforce or cancel.
body: Feynman diagrams for the same scattering process are likewise combined at amplitude level. Continuum invariant amplitudes additionally require flux and final-state phase-space factors to give cross sections; their squared values are not automatically probabilities.

lessons.title: Limit an integral before examining its behavior
lessons.idea: A cutoff puts a temporary upper limit on a troublesome sum.
body: A regulator can be a momentum cutoff, a lattice or dimensional regularization. Some regulators obscure symmetries, so consistent counterterms and checks are needed. The toy integral illustrates a logarithmic divergence rather than a complete loop calculation.

lessons.title: Fix a parameter using a measured reference
lessons.idea: Fix a calculation parameter by matching a known measurement.
body: A counterterm is the bookkeeping term that implements the required parameter adjustment in a perturbative calculation. The reference choice is a renormalization condition; agreement at the matching point alone does not establish predictive success elsewhere.

equationGuide.meaning: A calculated result may combine a regulator-dependent bare parameter and a loop correction. Match their sum to a measured reference. When the regulator changes, the bare parameter changes too, so the same reference result is kept. Predictions at other conditions then test the theory.

lessons.idea: An interaction’s quoted strength can change with the reference energy.
body: For four-dimensional real φ⁴ theory with ℒ_int = −λφ⁴/4!, the weak-coupling one-loop result is β = 3λ²/(16π²) plus higher orders. Residual scale dependence in a truncated result can help assess missing terms, but is not a guaranteed error bound.
